title: Fix pending auto-update installing a stale build
description:
Fixes #8284

### Summary

When Positron finds a pending update and the user delays "Restart to Update," a second update published in the meantime was never picked up: the pending update just stayed pending until restart, at which point it installed the stale build and immediately found a newer one. This PR makes the pending-update path re-check the feed instead of assuming what it staged is still current:

- The overwrite check (`checkForOverwriteUpdates`) now runs on a recurring interval while `Ready`, on explicit "Check for Updates" (also allowed from the `Ready` state, not just `Idle`), and again right before `quitAndInstall` -- so a restart can't install a build the feed has already superseded.
- Comparisons against the feed disable Chromium's HTTP cache (`disableCache: true`), which was letting a stale feed response look authoritative.
- On a metered connection, the overwrite check is deferred (not silently dropped) and re-attempted once the connection is no longer metered.
- Win32's `supportsUpdateOverwrite` is re-enabled (disabled in #16083 as a stopgap, since the overwrite round used to strand a pending update by clearing it without a way back); a new `restorePendingUpdate()` puts the original pending update back whenever the overwrite round doesn't produce a newer one.
- Adds dev-only tooling to exercise the whole flow without waiting for two real builds to ship: a mock update feed server (`npm run mock-update-server`, or the **Mock Update Server** task), a `devUpdateTesting` mode that simulates the download/install states on an unsigned source build, and a **Developer: Stage Pending Update from Feed URL...** command to stage an arbitrary hosted build as pending. See `scripts/mock-update-server/README.md` for the full walkthrough.

### Release Notes

#### New Features
- N/A

#### Bug Fixes
- Fix Positron installing a stale update after a newer one was published while a "Restart to Update" was pending (#8284)

### Validation Steps

Signed builds of this branch, for testing the real download/install flow rather than `devUpdateTesting`'s simulation:
- https://github.com/posit-dev/positron-builds/actions/runs/35229762744
- https://github.com/posit-dev/positron-builds/actions/runs/35232431766

@:update

Unit coverage: `positronQuitAndInstall.vitest.ts` and `positronIsLatestVersion.vitest.ts` exercise the overwrite check, the metered-connection deferral, and `quitAndInstall`'s pre-restart re-check.

Manual, against the mock feed (no signed build needed):

1. Add to a gitignored `product.overrides.json` at the repo root:
   ```json
   { "quality": "dev", "updateUrl": "http://localhost:8902/positron" }
   ```
2. Run the **Mock Update Server** task (or `npm run mock-update-server`), then launch Positron with `./scripts/code.sh`. Within 30s the tooltip reads **Restart to Update**.
3. Publish a newer version while Positron is still running:
   ```bash
   curl localhost:8902/publish/2026.09.0-3/bbbbbbb
   ```
4. Either wait up to 30s or click **Restart to Update** -- it should re-check first, pass through **Downloading Newer Update**, and settle back on **Restart to Update** with the new version instead of installing the stale one.
5. Click **Restart to Update** again; the main log should record it would install the newer version.

On macOS/Windows with a signed build, **Developer: Stage Pending Update from Feed URL...** can stage an older hosted build as pending and then verify the real overwrite/download round completes against the actual channel feed.

title: e2e: wait for the Jupyter server to stop before restarting it in teardown
description:
Fixes the four `[e2e-jupyter]` first-attempt failures in the 2026-09-18 positron-builds nightly (data-explorer-python-pandas, bootstrap-extensions, layouts, plots), all of which failed at 0ms in fixture start.

### Summary

The Jupyter fixture's teardown stops the single-user server, restarts it, and logs out so the next file starts clean. `stopServer()` clicked "Stop My Server" and only waited for `networkidle`, but the Positron server takes longer than JupyterHub's 10s slow-stop timeout to exit. `startServer()` then timed out waiting for "Start My Server", the teardown logged "Failed to stop Jupyter session" and skipped logout, and the next file's worker signed in while the server was still stopping. JupyterHub parks that sign-in on its "Your server is stopping" page, so `openPositron()` never saw the launcher card. The retry passed because the server had finished stopping by then.

Changes, all under `test/e2e/`:

- `stopServer()` waits for the hub to answer the stop request, then reloads the control panel until it renders without "Stop My Server". The hub renders that button whenever the spawner is active, including while stopping, so its absence is the real "stopped" signal. Bounded at 120s.
- `openPositron()` accepts either the launcher card or the "Your server is stopping" page after sign-in. In the latter case it reloads until the server is gone (the hub does not refresh that page itself), which redirects through the spawn handler and lands in JupyterLab. This covers a previous worker whose teardown was killed before it could stop the server.
- The fixture teardown logs the caught error at error level and says what the next worker will see, instead of a warning.

Evidence and mechanism write-up: nightly run https://github.com/posit-dev/positron-builds/actions/runs/35330437948, report https://d38p2avprg8il3.cloudfront.net/playwright-report-35330437948-1-jupyter-ubuntu-ubuntu/index.html.

title: New Folder from Git: let the destination folder be named
description:
Fixes #16077

### Summary

"New Folder from Git" had no way to name the folder a repository clones into. The name always came from the repository URL, and a collision with an existing folder was resolved silently by appending `-1`, `-2`. Cloning a fork under a distinct name meant renaming afterward or dropping to the command line.

This adds a **Folder name** field. It fills in from the repository URL and keeps following it until you type a name of your own; clearing the field puts it back under the URL's control. The name is validated as a folder name -- no path separators, plus the checks the New Folder flow already uses -- and a collision with an existing folder is now reported in the dialog.

The derivation lives in `newFolderFromGitFolderName.ts` and mirrors `Git.clone()`'s exactly, including its `repository` fallback for a URL whose last segment is nothing but `.git`. That parity is the point: leaving the pre-filled name alone lands the clone where it would have landed before the field existed.

`Git.clone()` already honored `options.targetName`, so the plumbing is three pass-throughs in the git extension -- `CloneOptions`, `CloneManager.cloneRepository`, and the `git.clone` command. Those are upstream files, so the edits are wrapped in Positron markers and the replaced lines kept as comments.

One deliberate behavior change: the silent `-1` / `-2` suffixing is gone for this dialog. A collision now blocks OK with "A folder named 'x' already exists." The issue offered either that or keeping the suffixing; this takes the first, on the grounds that a name you chose should be the name you get.

### Screenshots

https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/09824eb3-3109-43c7-ad73-10bd44faba4a

### Release Notes

#### New Features

- New Folder from Git lets you name the folder the repository is cloned into, instead of always using the repository's own name (#16077)

#### Bug Fixes

- N/A

### Validation Steps

@:new-folder-flow @:scm

1. **File > New Folder from Git...**
2. Paste a repository URL. "Folder name" should fill in with the repository's name as you type, and keep following the URL as you edit it.
3. Type your own name, then edit the URL again -- your name should stay. Clear the field and it should go back to following the URL.
4. Point the parent folder somewhere that already contains a folder of that name. The dialog should report the collision and refuse to clone, rather than quietly creating `<name>-1`.
5. Accept with a name of your own and confirm the clone lands in a folder with that name.

Unit coverage is 23 Vitest tests across two files: `newFolderFromGitFolderName.vitest.ts` (derivation parity with `Git.clone()` -- scp-style remotes, trailing separators, percent escapes, empty basenames) and `newFolderFromGitModalDialog.vitest.tsx` (pre-fill, tracking, stop-on-edit, resume-on-clear, whitespace-only input, collision reporting, and the name that actually reaches the clone).

Step 5 is the one thing unit tests don't reach since it needs a real remote.

title: e2e: wait for interpreter discovery before the venv prompt assertion
description:
### Summary Fixes a flake in the Python venv auto-creation e2e test, where the create-environment prompt arrived after the assertion had already timed out. - The prompt is gated on the python extension resolving the workspace's active interpreter, which waits on a full interpreter discovery pass. - `expectNoStartUpMessaging` returns well before discovery finishes, so the 60s toast wait was absorbing discovery time. - Waits on the picker's existing discovery-complete signal first, so the toast wait measures prompt latency only. - Test-only change; no product code touched. ### Release Notes #### New Features - N/A #### Bug Fixes - N/A ### Validation Steps @:interpreter @:web Runs on the ubuntu/chromium lane, where the flake was observed. On a run against the failing occurrence the prompt appeared ~94s after the folder opened, right as the 60s wait expired. ### E2E Triage Diagnosis
🟡 Medium confidence -- The create-env prompt is late, not suppressed: on attempt 1 the failure-time aria snapshot contains the requirements.txt/uv notification at the 60s expiry. The trigger gate passed (Welcome panel reports the workspace resolving to a global/system Python), so the failure is latency between folder open and the trigger completing its async gate, which awaits full Python env discovery. - **Test:** [Python Venv Auto-Creation > Clicking Yes creates venv](https://connect.posit.it/e2e-test-insights/?tab=test_health&repo=positron&test=Python%20Venv%20Auto-Creation%20%3E%20Clicking%20Yes%20creates%20venv%7C%7C%7Ctest%2Fe2e%2Ftests%2Finterpreters%2Fpython-venv-creation.test.ts) - **Targeted failure:** expect(locator).toBeVisible() failed - .notification-toast filtered on /requirements.txt/ - ubuntu/chromium - **Signal:** error-context attempt1 aria snapshot: alert "This project has requirements.txt but no virtual environment. Use uv to create a .venv..."; folder opened 20:12:29.8Z, toast wait 20:13:03.9-20:14:03.9Z; expectNoStartUpMessaging consumed 21-22s of Discovering interpreters messaging - **Frequency:** 3/59 runs (5.1%) on main, ubuntu/chromium - **Hypothesis:** createEnvironmentTrigger gate calls getActiveEnvironmentPath/resolveEnvironment, which awaits the full PET discovery refresh; on the slow ubuntu/chromium web lane that lands past the tests 60s window. PR #16033 does not flip the gate (conda-vs-global comparer rank unchanged; prompt did appear), but its RUNTIME_DISCOVERY_CACHE_SCHEMA_VERSION 3->4 bump forces one cold full discovery on the first launch after merge, which plausibly pushed the merge-commit run from flaky to hard failure. - **Supersedes:** PR #15039 (retry-safe folder opens) - recurred after merge

title: fix: order interpreter picker headings by environment source
description: Fixes #14803 ### Summary The interpreter/session picker ordered its environment-type headings by runtime registration order, which is discovery order, so System Pythons could sit above a workspace venv. An extension can't control that order, so the rank now travels on the runtime metadata and the picker sorts at read time. - Adds an optional `runtimeSourceOrder` to `LanguageRuntimeMetadata`, filled by positron-python from the same environment-type ranking that drives the Suggested entry. - The picker sorts its headings by that rank; unranked sources (e.g. R) follow the ranked ones, sorted by label so they don't shuffle between runs. - `positron-reticulate` ranks its Python too, or it would fall into the unranked bucket below `System`. - Adds `Pixi` to the priority table, where it was missing and so outranked everything, and ranks `Module`/`Custom` above `Global`/`System`. - Bumps the discovery cache schema to v4. The rank is persisted per entry, so a cache written on the old scale has to be discarded rather than replayed against freshly discovered runtimes. - The New Folder Flow interpreter dropdown sorts by the same rank, so the two lists agree. - The notebook kernel picker calls the same helper, so it inherits the fix. Heading order, top to bottom. Ranks are spaced by 10 so another extension can slot a source between two of them; `positron-reticulate` takes 135. | Rank | Source | | --- | --- | | 10 | `uv` | | 20 | `Poetry` | | 30 | `Pipenv` | | 40 | `Pixi` | | 50 | `VirtualEnvWrapper` | | 60 | `Hatch` | | 70 | `Venv` | | 80 | `VirtualEnv` | | 90 | `ActiveState` | | 100 | `Conda` | | 110 | `Pyenv` | | 120 | `Module` | | 130 | `Custom` | | 135 | `reticulate` | | 140 | `MicrosoftStore` | | 150 | `Global` | | 160 | `System` | | 170 | `Unknown` | Unchanged: the Suggested entry still comes from `getRecommended()`. #### Session Picker ##### Before https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/e02e04ca-a6cc-4abe-8d68-a227dbff3ea8 ##### After https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/e2f1fd83-8937-4926-8aa2-7a7d406a23a7 #### New Folder Flow ##### Before ##### After ### Release Notes #### New Features - N/A #### Bug Fixes - System Pythons are now listed last in the interpreter and session pickers, below uv, venv, conda and pyenv environments (#14803) ### Validation Steps @:interpreter @:sessions @:console @:new-folder-flow 1. Open a workspace that has its own `.venv`, on a machine with several system Pythons. 2. Run **Positron: Select Interpreter** (or start a new console session) and check the source headings: virtual-environment sources first, `Global` and `System` last. 3. Confirm the **Suggested** entry is still the workspace `.venv`. 4. In an R session, run `reticulate::repl_python()` so the reticulate runtime registers, then reopen the picker: `reticulate` sits below `Venv`/`Conda`/`Pyenv` and above `Global`/`System`. 5. Restart Positron and reopen the picker. The order must be the same on this warm start, when the discovery cache has already registered the system Pythons. 6. **New Folder** > **Python Project** > **Use an existing environment**: the interpreter dropdown has the same source order as the picker, with `System` last.

title: Run Workbench under supervisord in the e2e harness
description:
### Summary

The Workbench e2e harness now runs rserver and the session launcher under supervisord on every OS, the way Posit's own Workbench container images (`rstudio/rstudio-docker-products` and its successor `posit-dev/images-workbench`) run them. This replaces the packaged SysV init scripts, which cannot see their own processes inside a container without systemd: `stop` was a silent no-op, `restart` started a second rserver that wedged on nginx "Address already in use", and the EL9 launcher script never started anything. The harness had grown about 250 lines across three files to work around that (`pkill` with TERM-then-KILL escalation, bracketed `pgrep -f` patterns, `nohup setsid` for the launcher on Rocky, manual socket cleanup, a per-family choice of which init script to trust).

What changed:

- `install-workbench.sh` installs `supervisor` from the distro repos (Ubuntu universe, EPEL on Rocky, Leap main), so the shared CI images are untouched. It writes one complete config at `/etc/supervisord.conf` (first in `supervisorctl`'s default search path on all three OSes, so no `-c` anywhere) plus a small wrapper that waits for the launcher socket and then runs `rserver --server-daemonize 0`. Both programs have `autorestart=true`; rserver has `stopasgroup`/`killasgroup` so an orphaned `rserver-http` can no longer hold `:8787`. The `initscripts` / `sysvinit-tools` installs and the `extras/init.d` copying are gone.
- `workbench-local.sh`'s stop/resume path (`wb_ensure_workbench`) is now "start supervisord if it is not running, else `supervisorctl start all`", and readiness waits for both `:8787` and supervisord's `RUNNING` state.
- The CI action's post-swap restart and the enforced-settings test use `supervisorctl restart rstudio-server`. Only rserver is restarted; the launcher does not need the new build and restarting it would kill sessions.
- README documents the new layout; ROCKY-PLAN gets a note that its init-script findings are historical.

positron-builds needs no companion PR: its action copies the installer out of the submodule, and the config is written by the installer rather than shipped as a new file, so its enumerated copy list does not change.

Verified locally through `npm run pwb` on Ubuntu 24 and Rocky 9 (arm64 daily Workbench, daily Positron): fresh install, the CI-style `supervisorctl restart rstudio-server` (6 seconds back to a 302, exactly one rserver, no bind errors), `kill -9` of rserver (respawned within a second, no orphans), `stop` then resume, `--reinstall` over a running stack, and the three enforced-settings e2e tests passing on both OSes. The local openSUSE run (emulated amd64 on Apple Silicon) was still in flight when this PR opened; its result will be posted as a comment, and the openSUSE lane here is the native check.

### Release Notes

#### New Features
- N/A

#### Bug Fixes
- N/A

### Validation Steps

@:workbench-all @:workbench-stable

1. In the Ubuntu, Rocky and openSUSE lanes, the "Install Workbench in container" step should print `Starting Workbench...` followed by `rstudio-launcher: started` / `rstudio-server: started` from supervisord, with no `Stopping ... did not exit on TERM` lines after the first stop of the postinst-started daemons.
2. The "Install custom Positron build" step's restart should return in a few seconds; if it does not, the step now dumps `supervisorctl status` and the supervisor logs before failing.
3. The enforced-settings tests exercise the restart path twice per run and should pass on all three OSes. Expect exactly one red test on Rocky, the known `environment-modules` Python case (#15509), unrelated to this change.
4. Locally: `npm run pwb -- --os=<os> --workbench=daily --positron=daily`, then `docker exec test sudo supervisorctl status` shows both programs `RUNNING`; `npm run pwb -- stop && npm run pwb` comes back with `Workbench ready`.

title: ci: run the Workbench e2e lanes and shards one at a time
description:
When a PR carries tags for more than one Workbench lane, or the nightly full suite runs all four, the lanes start together. The managed-credential shards (snowflake, databricks, azure) all sign in with the same service-account TOTP secret, so overlapping sign-ins burn the same OTP window and the sign-in flakes.

### Summary

Mirrors the fix already landed in positron-builds (posit-dev/positron-builds#1208), which had two parts, not one:

- **Chain the lanes with `needs`** in `test-pull-request.yml` and `test-full-suite.yml`: Ubuntu, then Rocky, then openSUSE, then stable. A concurrency group would not work here: it holds only one pending entry and cancels the rest outright, which is what silently dropped the stable lane in positron-builds.
- **Cap the shard matrix at one shard at a time** in `test-e2e-workbench-linux.yml`. This repo's reusable workflow had no such cap, so the three credential shards inside a single Ubuntu lane were already colliding on their own, independent of how many lanes ran.

Because each PR lane is selected by its own tag, the chained lanes use `!cancelled()` plus an explicit `needs.build-workbench.result == 'success'` check instead of the default "all needs succeeded" rule. A lane behind a skipped or failed lane still runs; a failed or skipped Workbench build, or a cancelled run, still skips everything. In the full suite the chained lanes drop `!failure()` for the same explicit check, since `!failure()` would also fire when the lane ahead failed.

Trade-off: wall-clock time for multi-lane PRs and the nightly goes up, since lanes and shards now queue instead of overlapping.

Not covered: the desktop Ubuntu lane also uses this TOTP secret for the Snowflake data-connections test and the Posit Assistant Databricks test, so a PR carrying the connections or assistant tags alongside a Workbench tag can still collide there.

title: Let extensions control runtime session working directories
description:
Fixes #15985

Extensions can now start a runtime session in a chosen directory and inspect or change the directory of a session obtained through the Positron API. This supports clients such as Canvas that work in a different folder from the IDE window.

- Add optional `workingDirectory` to `positron.runtime.startLanguageRuntime`; it overrides notebook directory configuration when supplied.
- Expose `positron.runtime.getSessionWorkingDirectory(sessionId?)` and move `setWorkingDirectory` onto `BaseLanguageRuntimeSession`, including forwarding for sessions owned by another extension host.
- Preserve existing defaults and runtime lifecycle behavior. Concurrent starts can share a session, ignoring the later directory request with a warning. `setWorkingDirectory` acknowledges the request before the change necessarily completes; callers can verify the runtime-reported directory. Public API docs describe these semantics.

Paths are absolute on the runtime's machine and are passed through without expansion or existence checks. Console startup deferred for workspace trust and restart of an uninitialized session retain their existing defaults; callers needing a particular directory should recheck it. This PR adds no workspace-switching UI or modal changes.

### Release Notes

#### New Features

- Extensions can specify a runtime session's startup directory and inspect or change its working directory through the Positron API.

#### Bug Fixes

- N/A

### Validation Steps

@:sessions @:console @:notebooks

- Targeted Vitest suites: `mainThreadLanguageRuntime.vitest.ts` and `runtimeSession.vitest.ts`, **186 passed, 5 skipped**. Coverage includes console startup directory, explicit notebook override, concurrent-start coalescing and warning, query behavior, setter forwarding, and unknown sessions.
- Public API smoke tests in a separate development instance with a temporary extension/profile, using real R and Python: explicit startup directory agrees with executed code; `getSession().setWorkingDirectory()` changes the directory and preserves variables; active/foreground session access and foreground directory query work; omitted console directory retains the workspace default; omitted notebook directory follows `notebook.workingDirectory`; unknown-session query returns `undefined`. Test-owned sessions were shut down.
- Client compilation: zero errors. Precommit checks pass for all changed files.
- Broader local checks remain non-green outside this diff: the test TypeScript project reports 383 diagnostics, none in changed files; the E2E watcher lacks `archiver`, `ncp`, `canvas`, and `resemblejs` dependencies.

To verify manually, create two scratch directories, start an R or Python console with the first as the fourth argument to `startLanguageRuntime`, and compare `getSessionWorkingDirectory(session.metadata.sessionId)` with executed `getwd()` / `os.getcwd()`. Set a variable, change to the second directory through a session returned by `getSession`, wait for the reported directory to update, and confirm the variable remains available. Also verify ordinary console startup and notebook directory configuration.

title: Stop the overwrite check from cancelling every pending Windows update
description:
On Windows a background update stages itself and then waits for Positron to exit. Five minutes after every `Ready` state, `checkForOverwriteUpdates()` asks `isLatestVersion()` whether the staged build is still current, and discards it when the answer is `false`.

The answer was always `false`. So a "Restart to Update" notification left sitting for five minutes silently threw the staged update away and started the download over. Clicking Restart after that point exited without updating and came back on the old build, which is the symptom in #13988.

This is a **second, independent cause** of that issue. #15469 fixed the flag-ordering race and is intact; this is the part it did not reach.

### Evidence

From a `%TEMP%\Setup Log` on a daily, two runs for the same target build:

```
10:02:38.127  Checking whether application is still running...
10:07:38.874  Cancel file detected, aborting background update.
```

Exactly 5:00.8 after the wait loop opened, matching the `overwriteUpdatesCheckInterval` armed in `setState()`. It never logs `Application appears not to be running.`, so Positron was still up. The next run, quit inside the five-minute window, swapped and relaunched normally.

### Cause

`isLatestVersion()` was wrong twice over, and the two defects partly cancelled - which is how this survived review:

1. It compared the feed against bare `positronVersion`. `compare()` in `positronVersion.ts` treats two versions as equal when either side omits the build number, so every same-month daily looked like the same build.
2. It returned `hasUpdate()`, which is true when a *newer* build exists - the opposite of what the name promises.

Fixing either one alone stops the cancel, so a half-fix looks like it works.

The two also made the no-argument callers wrong in both directions: someone already on the newest build was reported as "not latest" (suppressing startup-timing telemetry in `startupTimings`), while someone a month behind was reported as "latest".

`isLatestVersion()` became reachable from `checkForOverwriteUpdates()` in the 1.111.0 merge (#12996). Before that it was dead code, which is why "Compare build numbers" (#6011) fixed the sibling call site and missed this one.

### Changes

- Compare against `commit ?? currentVersion`, and return `!hasUpdate(...)`. Honoring the argument is what makes the overwrite check ask its real question - has the feed moved past what we staged - rather than never firing.
- Report an unknown answer as `undefined` rather than `false`. The request and JSON parse are now awaited inside the `try`: a returned promise settles after the block exits, so a failed request, unparseable JSON, or the `hasUpdate()` throw on a malformed version used to reject. `startupTimings` and `timerService` both `await` this unguarded.
- Add a `currentVersion` getter so the `<version>-<build>` string has one definition. Three hand-built copies are how the call sites drifted apart.
- Drop the stale `@ts-ignore - unused but kept for upstream compatibility` on `checkForOverwriteUpdates()`; it has been called since 1.111.0, so the suppression does nothing and removing it leaves the declaration identical to upstream.

Net, the first commit **removes** three lines of Positron fencing and adds none - every new line sits inside an existing fence. The notes on `isLatestVersion()` go inside the Positron block that already opens on its first body line, rather than in a JSDoc above an upstream signature.

`isLatestVersion()` keeps upstream's `commit` parameter name and signature. Positron's feed is versioned rather than commit-addressed, and the comment says so; renaming would only add a merge conflict. The unused `token` is deliberately left alone - wiring it would abort the request on the caller's 2s timeout and log an error every five minutes on a slow feed, which wants its own change.

### Second commit: fence hygiene

`abstractUpdateService.ts` had two unbalanced markers, both predating this branch: a `Start` above `checkForUpdates()` that never closed, and an `End` before the closing brace with no `Start`. Neither changes behavior, but upstream merges read these markers to tell our code from upstream's. The file now nests to depth 0.

`updateService.win32.ts` is unbalanced too (17 `Start` to 19 `End`). Untouched here; it wants its own pass.

### Release Notes

#### New Features

- N/A

#### Bug Fixes

- Positron no longer discards a downloaded Windows update while it waits for you to restart (#13988)

### Validation Steps

@:win @:critical

```
npx vitest run src/vs/platform/update/test/electron-main/positronIsLatestVersion.vitest.ts
```

Six cases covering both defects and both failure paths. Every one was verified to fail against the previous implementation - three of the four original cases fail there, which is the honest number, since the two old defects cancel in the "feed has moved past the staged build" case.

A dev build does not run the real installer, so **the end-to-end check needs a daily build after merge**:

1. Let an update download and reach "Restart to Update".
2. Wait more than five minutes.
3. Choose "Restart to Update".

The newest `%TEMP%\Setup Log *.txt` must log `Application appears not to be running.` followed by `inno_updater completed with result code 0`. Before this change it logged `Cancel file detected, aborting background update.` exactly five minutes after `Checking whether application is still running...`.

title: e2e: add Snowflake catalog explorer case and run the suite on Workbench
description:
### Summary

Adds a Snowflake case to the catalog explorer e2e suite and runs the suite on Workbench as well as desktop and web.

The new case writes a `connections.toml` for the shared Snowflake test user (password auth, set explicitly so the provider does not fall back to an External Browser sign-in), adds the provider through the Add Catalog Provider command, and asserts the `FINANCIAL__ECONOMIC_ESSENTIALS` Marketplace share appears in the tree. On Workbench the file is copied into the container, since the extension host there cannot see the host filesystem, and removed again after the suite so other suites sharing the container are unaffected.

Suite changes that apply to both cases:

- Both catalog explorer settings are baked in via `extraSettings` before the app starts, so the `beforeAll` restart is gone on every platform. The Snowflake connections path is chosen per project (a host temp dir, or `/home/user1/.snowflake` in the container).
- The Catalog Explorer section is expanded only when it is collapsed. The header click is a toggle, and the tree renders nothing while the section is collapsed, which is why a provider that authenticated in under a second never appeared.
- Assertions are scoped to the tree, so the closed quick pick's hidden "Snowflake" row can no longer match.
- An `afterEach` collapses all providers. The section only has room for a few rows and the tree is virtualized, so without this the second case's databases sit below the first case's catalogs and never render.

Workflow changes:

- The Workbench lane exports `DATABRICKS_WORKSPACE` and `DATABRICKS_PAT` for the existing Databricks case.
- The Windows and macOS lanes export `SNOWFLAKE_USER` and `SNOWFLAKE_PASSWORD` so the Snowflake case runs there instead of skipping.
- `.env.e2e-workbench.example` documents the two Databricks variables.

### Release Notes

#### New Features
- N/A

#### Bug Fixes
- N/A

### Validation Steps

@:catalog-explorer @:web @:win @:workbench

Both cases pass locally on `e2e-electron` and `e2e-workbench`. In CI, check that the Snowflake case runs (not skips) on the Windows and macOS lanes, which confirms those runners can read the two Snowflake secrets, and that the Databricks case passes on the Workbench lane with the newly exported workspace and PAT.

- New `scripts/quickpick-enum.sh`: enumerate a quick pick by keyboard, since the DOM holds only a ~10-row window.
- New `scripts/reseed.sh`: reuse a stopped instance's profile, so warm-start paths like discovery cache replay are reachable.

title: ci: skip Graphviz install and graphviz plot tests on macOS x64
description:
## Summary

The scheduled macOS x64 e2e job has failed at **Setup Graphviz** on every run since 2026-09-08 (see the positron-builds daily release, e.g. [this job](https://github.com/posit-dev/positron-builds/actions/runs/34817929854/job/103929598859)). The same step runs in this repo's `test-full-suite` macOS x64 job.

Root cause: Homebrew dropped x86_64 bottles in September 2026. `brew install graphviz` on the Intel runner now compiles graphviz and ~20 dependencies from source (rust alone takes 40 minutes, the step went from 76 s to 61 min) and then exits 1 anyway, because the netpbm formula fetches its source over svn before subversion is installed:

```
✘ Resource netpbm--html
##[error]You must: brew install svn
```

## Changes

- `test-e2e-macos-run.yml`: gate the **Setup Graphviz** step on `inputs.arch != 'x64'`.
- `plots.test.ts`: skip the two tests that render through the `dot` binary (`Static Plot`, `Plot actions`) when `process.platform === 'darwin' && process.arch === 'x64'`.

Coverage for those two tests remains on macOS arm64, Linux, and Windows. Apple has dropped Intel support in macOS 27 and GitHub is retiring Intel runners in 2027, so this is a coverage trade rather than a permanent fix.

Companion PR in positron-builds gates the same step in `test-e2e-macos-release.yml`.

## QA Notes

- Run the macOS x64 e2e job: Setup Graphviz should be skipped and the two graphviz plot tests reported as skipped.
- Run the macOS arm64 e2e job: no change.

title: Make extension-contributed action bar checkboxes accessible
description: Fixes #7289 ### Summary This PR improves the accessibility of checkboxes contributed by extensions to the Editor Action Bar. The checkbox now: - Exposes a consistent accessible name, role, checked state, and disabled state. - Supports Space and Enter activation through the shared `Button` component. - Includes its visible label in the clickable area while presenting the checkbox as a single control to assistive technology. - Follows the extension's context-key state instead of maintaining an optimistic local copy. - Updates when the extension changes its checked state externally. - Uses native button disablement when its command is unavailable. This also adds an Action Bar Controls entry to the Control Gallery for inspecting the checkbox's checked, disabled, and labelled states. The Editor Action Bar's existing focus and arrow-navigation behavior is outside the scope of this PR. ### Screenshots https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/540c0cf9-678c-44f3-a4b5-b2a9949b8d9d ### Release Notes #### New Features - N/A #### Bug Fixes - Extension-contributed Editor Action Bar checkboxes now expose their label, checked state, disabled state, and keyboard interaction correctly to assistive technology. (#7289) ### Validation Steps @:editor-action-bar @:quarto #### Control Gallery 1. Run **Open Control Gallery**. 2. Select **Action Bar Controls**. 3. Verify changing the **Label** updates both the visible and accessible names. 4. Verify the **Checked** control updates the checkmark and `aria-checked` state. 5. Verify clicking either the box or visible label toggles the checkbox once. 6. Focus the enabled checkbox and verify Space and Enter each toggle it once. 7. Enable **Disabled** and verify the checkbox is dimmed, skipped by Tab, and cannot be activated. 8. Hover the checkbox and verify its tooltip uses the current label. #### VoiceOver 1. On macOS, open the **Action Bar Controls** gallery and start VoiceOver with Command+F5. 2. Navigate to the checkbox with Control+Option+Right Arrow. 3. Verify VoiceOver announces the checkbox's current label, checkbox role, and checked or unchecked state as one control. 4. Activate the checkbox with Control+Option+Space. 5. Verify VoiceOver announces the updated checked state and does not announce the visible label or checkmark as separate nested elements. 6. Change the **Label** field and navigate back to the checkbox. Verify VoiceOver announces the new label. 7. Enable **Disabled** and navigate back to the checkbox using VoiceOver. Verify it is announced as disabled and cannot be activated. #### Quarto 1. Open a `.qmd` file that displays the **Render on Save** checkbox. 2. Verify its initial checked state matches the Quarto setting. 3. Click the checkbox and verify its checkmark and accessible checked state update. 4. Open the Command Palette and run **Quarto: Render on Save**. 5. Verify the existing checkbox updates without reopening the editor. 6. Verify the checkbox's enabled state follows the command enablement supplied by Quarto. ### QA Notes For extension-contributed controls, a command's `enablement` expression becomes its precondition. Positron uses that precondition to determine whether the action is enabled, and the checkbox now reflects that state using native disabled behavior. The Quarto extension therefore needs to update the **Render on Save** command's `enablement` expression to include every editor where the checkbox should be interactive. Until then, the checkbox may appear disabled in some Quarto editors. CC @juliasilge, who plans to make this change in the Quarto extension.

description:
Fixes #15442

Currently, all seven `positron-data-driver-*` extensions activate together on the `onView:workbench.panel.positronDataConnections` event. Four of them (Databricks, Snowflake, PostgreSQL, and Redshift) imported their database SDK at the top of a client module. The `activate()` function reaches that module synchronously, so the pane therefore loaded `@databricks/sql`, `snowflake-sdk`, `pg`, and three `@aws-sdk` packages at activation. A user who, for example, only opens SQLite connections paid this cost too.

This PR moves each SDK behind a dynamic `import()` in the client factory. The cost now moves from pane activation to the first connection attempt, which I think is better. SQLite, DuckDB, and ODBC do not have this problem, because they keep their native module in a worker process.

The linked issue outlines two possible fixes, and this PR takes the first approach. All seven extensions still activate, but activation now costs only the registration of a metadata object. I think it solves the problem sufficiently that we don't need to do anything else for now.

### Performance

The table below gives the time to load each driver bundle. I measured it on the packaged macOS arm64 build, with `vscode` and `positron` stubbed. This is that "extra"  cost the extension host pays at activation.

| Driver | Before | After | Deferred to first connect |
|---|---|---|---|
| Databricks | 79 ms | 1.2 ms | 83 ms |
| Snowflake | 143 ms | 2.0 ms | 144 ms |
| PostgreSQL | 6.5 ms | 1.2 ms | 12 ms |
| Redshift | 19 ms | 1.2 ms | 10 ms, plus the AWS SDK on IAM connections |
| **Total** | **248 ms** | **5.6 ms** | |

The last column shows that the cost is just moved, but now a user who never opens a Redshift connection never loads the AWS SDK and a Redshift user with password authentication does not ever load it either.

`pg` and the AWS SDK are now esbuild externals, so they load from `node_modules` on demand. Before this change they were bundled and also shipped in `node_modules`. Removing that duplicate copy makes the PostgreSQL bundle 81 KB smaller and the Redshift bundle 451 KB smaller.

### Release Notes

#### New Features
- N/A

#### Bug Fixes
- The Data Connections pane opens faster, because each database SDK now waits to load on the first connection (#15442)

### Validation Steps

@:connections

The E2E suite covers all four drivers in `test/e2e/tests/data-connections/`. Each driver also has a new unit test for its real client factory. That test fails if a lazy import does not give the expected export.

It would be best to do these steps on a release build and not a dev build:

1. Open the Data Connections pane. Make sure that all seven drivers appear in the Add Connection dialog.
2. Generate a connection code snippet for the drivers, without a connection.
3. Run _Developer: Show Running Extensions_ with the pane open. Each of the four drivers should activate in 1 ms to 5 ms.
4. Connect to Snowflake and run a query. This is the most important manual validation, because the compiler cannot catch an error in it.
5. Connect to Databricks and run a query.
6. Connect to PostgreSQL in single-database mode. Then connect again in server mode, which uses a second factory path.
7. Connect to Redshift with password authentication.
8. Connect to Redshift with IAM authentication. This is the only path that loads the AWS SDK.
9. Connect to PostgreSQL. Restart the server. Then run a query. The connection must recover without an error.

Step 8 matters most, because the Redshift IAM path holds the only new code in this PR and I have not run that myself yet.

title: e2e: settle the assistant greeting before trusting a skipped new-conversation click
description:
Fixes the "Sign in with an API key, send hello, sign out" (Snowflake Cortex) hard failure on chromium in [run 34631121008](https://github.com/posit-dev/positron/actions/runs/34631121008), and the same-shaped flakes in the anthropic-api sign-in and welcome-page tests on that shard.

The Posit Assistant webview paints the fresh/greeting state first and restores the last persisted conversation about 100-300ms later (machine-wide store, see #15187). Since #16006, `startNewConversation` samples `isEnabled()` on the `+` button once; in that pre-hydration window a released build reports it disabled, the click is skipped, and the restored conversation then replaces the greeting. On the first attempt the welcome-title expect timed out; on the retry it passed inside the same window and the test typed into the sign-in suite's old "Say hello" chat, which is where the strict-mode error listing three assistant messages came from.

Changes to `test/e2e/pages/positAssistant.ts`:

- `startNewConversation` now wraps click + greeting check in `toPass()` and requires the greeting to survive a 1s settle window. If a restored conversation lands over it, the retry sees an enabled button and performs a real click.
- `expectResponseVisible` targets the last assistant message so multi-turn conversations (and the persona greeting, which renders as an assistant message) do not trip strict mode.

### Release Notes

#### New Features
- N/A

#### Bug Fixes
- N/A

### Validation Steps

@:assistant @:web

The assistant suites should pass on both the electron and chromium lanes. The web lane is the one that reproduced the race.

title: Reshape the data connections commands for the positron-commands skill
description:
Fixes #15592. Part of #15343; implements the skill side of the plan in #14664.

### Summary

Documents the data connections commands in the positron-commands skill, and reshapes the commands themselves around how Assistant actually uses them:

- **New reference file** `references/data-connections.md` in the positron-commands skill template: when to call each command, the two-panes distinction (Data Connections vs. session Connections), why running code can't find configured profiles, and the payload-level failure shapes.
- **`positronDataConnections.getConnections` is now a compact catalog.** Each profile returns `profileId`, `connected`, and a single self-describing `summary` line (name, driver, mechanism, languages, redacted parameters) instead of a field-per-fact object with generated code. This avoids a driver round trip per profile per language on every "what connections do I have?" call.
- **The catalog now covers connections detected on the machine, not just saved ones.** It reports the full pane catalog -- saved profiles first, then the connections drivers discover (e.g. ODBC data sources), marked `discovered=true` with the driver's own one-line description. Their `profileId`s work with `getConnectionCode` and `getSchema` like any other, so Assistant can answer "what connections do I have?" on a machine where the user has saved nothing yet. Ephemeral, so the reference tells callers to re-read the catalog rather than store an id.
- **New `positronDataConnections.getConnectionCode` command** generates the secret-free connection code for one named profile (optionally one language), with typed unavailable reasons (`disabled`, `not-found`, `no-driver`, `no-code` -- the last naming the languages the driver does support).
- **`positronDataConnections.getSchema` now auto-connects** a non-live target (named, or the only saved profile when nothing is live), with new reasons `not-found`, `no-driver`, `connect-failed`, `no-connections`, and `ambiguous` now listing `candidateProfileIds`. Its output switched from a nested node tree to compact one-line-per-object rendering with columns folded onto their table's line, roughly halving payload size.
- **New "Show Connection Code as JSON" Command Palette entry**, alongside the existing catalog and schema inspect actions. The schema action still never opens a connection of its own.
- **Catalog parameter values now go through driver redaction wholesale.** Every parameter is offered to the driver's `redactParameterValue`, not only the ones its mechanism declares secret, and a discovered connection's held-aside secret values are redacted the same way a saved profile's are. Nothing leaks today -- the one parameter that embeds a credential (`connectionString`) is already declared secret and already redacted by the ODBC and PostgreSQL drivers -- so this closes a contract gap for a future or third-party driver rather than fixing a live problem.
- **A discovery the user saved is now matched by provenance, not by guessing.** `saveDiscoveredProfile` records which discovery a profile came from, so the discovery stays suppressed after the profile is renamed or edited. A connection configured by hand is still matched by driver, mechanism, name, and values; the name is in that match because the values that would distinguish two same-shaped data sources are the secret ones held out of both profiles.
- A frontmatter validator test for all skill templates, guarding the Assistant's name/description limits.

### Release Notes

#### New Features

- Assistant can now read the data connections you have configured and the ones Positron detects on your machine, fetch the code that opens one, and browse a connection's schema -- connecting it automatically when it is not live yet (#15592)

#### Bug Fixes

- N/A

### Validation Steps

@:connections

Unit coverage is in `positronDataConnectionsCommands.vitest.ts`, `positronDataConnectionsInspectActions.vitest.ts`, `dataConnectionSchemaSummary.vitest.ts`, `positronDataConnectionsService.vitest.ts`, and `agentSkillFrontmatter.vitest.ts` (`npm run test:positron`).

To validate manually:

1. Configure a data connection (e.g. SQLite) from the Data Connections panel, without connecting it.
2. Run "Data Connections: Show Connections as JSON" from the Command Palette -- each profile should show `profileId`, `connected`, and a one-line `summary` with secrets redacted.
3. With an ODBC DSN configured on the machine, confirm it appears in that same output after the saved profiles, marked `discovered=true` with a `description`.
4. Run "Data Connections: Show Connection Code as JSON" -- the generated code per language should appear, with no secrets.
5. Ask Assistant "what tables does my connection have?" -- getSchema should connect the profile automatically and return one compact line per schema object, with columns folded onto their table's line.
6. Toggle `dataConnections.enabled` off and confirm the palette entries disappear and the commands report `disabled` / an empty list.
7. Save the discovered ODBC row from the pane, then rename the saved profile -- the discovered row should stay hidden. Adding another connection by hand under a different name should leave the discovery visible rather than hiding it.

title: e2e: require a better-ranked Python source when versions collide
description:
### Summary A Packages pane test flaked because the Python session sometimes started on a uv-managed base interpreter instead of the uv venv, and `pip install` is refused there under PEP 668 -- so the package never showed up in the list. - The runtime quick pick reports discovery complete before every runtime has registered. - Three interpreters report 3.10.12 on Linux CI, and the uv venv registered 4.2s after the session started. - Prefer a better-ranked interpreter source when several rows share a version, retrying instead of taking the base install. - Keep the existing fallback where only one interpreter of that version exists (a Pyenv alternate, System Python on Windows). - Fail at selection when the started session isn't the one picked, instead of as a later install timeout. ### QA Notes Touches `sessions.start()`, so the blast radius is every test that starts a session. @:packages-pane @:interpreter @:sessions @:web @:win ### E2E Triage Diagnosis
🟢 High confidence -- openFolder's window reload restarts interpreter discovery; the picker's discovery-complete signal fires before the intended uv venv runtime registers, so the session starts on a uv-managed base Python where PEP 668 makes pip install fail. - **Test:** [Packages Pane > Python - Install, search, and uninstall package > Python - Install, search, and uninstall package (python)](https://connect.posit.it/e2e-test-insights/?tab=test_health&repo=positron&test=Packages%20Pane%20%3E%20Python%20-%20Install%2C%20search%2C%20and%20uninstall%20package%20%3E%20Python%20-%20Install%2C%20search%2C%20and%20uninstall%20package%20%28python%29%7C%7C%7Ctest%2Fe2e%2Ftests%2Fpackages-pane%2Fpackages-pane.test.ts) - **Targeted failure:** Error: expect(locator).toBeVisible() failed -- Locator: locator('.positron-packages-list').locator('.packages-list-item-name').filter({ hasText: 'cowsay' }).first(); Expected: visible; Timeout: 60000ms; element(s) not found - **Signal:** verifyPackagesList passes with rows present, then the install is dispatched and the packages list drops to zero rows for the entire 60s wait. The trace shows the 'Installing packages...' toast appearing normally, but the raw PTY bytes carry pip's real output: 'error: externally-managed-environment / This Python installation is managed by uv'. The session had started at 20:36:46.416 on 'Python 3.10.12 (Global)' = /root/.local/share/uv/python/cpython-3.10-linux-x86_64-gnu/bin/python, while the intended 'Python 3.10.12 (uv: root)' = /root/.venv/bin/python did not finish registering until 20:36:50.612 -- 4.2s after selection. runtimeSource 'Global' routes packageManagerFactory.ts:37 to PipPackageManager instead of UvPackageManager, and pip into a uv-managed base install can never succeed. - **Frequency:** 4/145 runs (2.8%) on main, ubuntu/electron - **Hypothesis:** race

title: Disable Playwright snapshots in performance tests
description:
Part of https://github.com/posit-dev/positron/issues/15466

The difference between R and Python came from this interaction:

- The R test runs after the Python trim test, after which the console contains thousands of lines.
- Playwright snapshoting captures the DOM, which now contains those python lines

Disabling snapshots drastically reduced the difference in local tests.

This doesn't explain the end of July step in R timings, but it should make measurements easier to interpret.

Other change: `expectPromptReady()` removes an unnecessary key chord from the measured test. Claude thinks this could pollute measurements as well.

title: fix(e2e): dismiss toasts before New Folder Flow modal clicks
description:
### Summary Fixes a flaky "New env: uv environment" e2e failure where a background session's notification toast (e.g. a forwarded-port notice) renders over the New Folder Flow modal and intercepts clicks for the full timeout. - `NewFolderFlow.clickFlowButton` now dismisses open toasts before clicking any flow button - Reuses the existing `Toasts` helper via constructor injection, matching the pattern already used by `Modals`, `Assistant`, `ModelProviderModal`, and `Packages` - Also fixes an indexing bug in `Toasts.closeAll()` itself: it snapshotted the toast count once and closed by position, so closing one toast could shift a later one out from under the next index, skipping it when multiple toasts were open at once. `closeAll()` is shared by several other suites (packages pane, notebooks, plots, assistant), so this PR tags those areas too as a sanity check on the shared helper. ### Release Notes #### New Features - N/A #### Bug Fixes - N/A ### QA Notes @:new-folder-flow @:modal @:packages-pane @:positron-notebooks @:plots @:assistant ### E2E Triage Diagnosis
🟢 High confidence -- clickFlowButton(CREATE) times out because a background notification toast (forwarded-port info alert from an earlier subtest session in the same window) overlaps the New Folder Flow modal and intercepts pointer events on the Create button for the full 30s. - **Test:** [New Folder Flow: Python Project > New env: uv environment](https://connect.posit.it/e2e-test-insights/?tab=test_health&repo=positron&test=New%20Folder%20Flow%3A%20Python%20Project%20%3E%20New%20env%3A%20uv%20environment%7C%7C%7Ctest%2Fe2e%2Ftests%2Fnew-folder-flow%2Fnew-folder-flow-python.test.ts) - **Targeted failure:** locator.click: Timeout 30000ms exceeded on the New Folder Flow Create button - **Signal:** Playwright call log shows every retry blocked by ".notification-toast-container" / ".notifications-toasts bottom-right visible" intercepting pointer events; page snapshot at failure shows the open toast ("Your application running on port 5877 is available") plus 16 accumulated forwarded ports from prior New env subtests in the same window, while the modal Create button itself is visible/enabled/stable throughout. - **Frequency:** 2/116 runs (1.7%) on main, ubuntu/chromium - **Hypothesis:** distinct from PR #15029 (dropped CREATED_VENV marker, no console start) despite git-ancestry flagging this occurrence as postdating that fix -- console/session here started fine; the blocker is a stray toast, a timing coincidence between a background session's port-forward notification and this test's modal click, not a recurrence of the marker race

title: DEBUG: fingerprint the Jupyter CI license file
description:
Temporary debug PR -- do not merge.

Adds a step to the `setup-jupyter-docker` action that prints sha256 hashes of the
license as delivered by the `POSITRON_LICENSE` secret and of the `license.lic` that
actually lands in the container. Hashes only; the raw value is a masked secret and
is never echoed.

Two hashes of the secret on purpose: the existing step writes the file with `echo`,
which appends a newline, so the container copy may not be byte-identical to the
secret value. The pair shows which form actually landed.

Read the hash from the "DEBUG - fingerprint license" step in the `e2e / jupyter` job.

title: Welcome Page Feedback

description:
Fixes #15989

This PR fixes the welcome page scrollbar becoming stale when dynamically rendered content changes height. The page now remeasures its content and updates the scrollbar whenever environment checks, expandable sections, or other dynamic content change its height.

The resize observer is tied to the welcome page's lifecycle, so it is disconnected whenever the page is rebuilt or closed.

### Screenshots

**BEFORE**

https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/275d6d56-db70-4eb3-af7a-61d8ca6e9a21

**AFTER**

https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/791bdf65-e26a-4d02-a9d0-89af2acdc951

### Release Notes

#### New Features

- N/A

#### Bug Fixes

- Fixed welcome page controls becoming unreachable after expanding environment setup details (#15989)

### Validation Steps

@:welcome

Manual:

1. Open the welcome page in a window short enough for the page to scroll.
2. Scroll to the bottom and confirm the startup checkbox is visible.
3. Expand a successful R or Python environment setup group.
4. Confirm the scrollbar updates and the startup checkbox remains reachable.
5. Collapse the group and confirm the scrollbar range shrinks without excess blank space.

title: Remember the last plot save directory for the current session
description:
Fixes #2841

Remember the last directory used to save a plot during the current Positron session, so subsequent plot exports reuse that directory instead of falling back to the working directory.

This keeps the scope intentionally narrow and aligned with the issue discussion:
- the remembered directory lives only in the plots service for the current session
- it is reused by both the dynamic plot save modal and the static plot save dialog
- it is not persisted across restarts or workspaces

title: Data connections connect with ggsql
description:
# Add ggsql "Connect With" support to Data Connections drivers

Adds ggsql as a "Connect With" language option alongside Python and R, and fixes a bug uncovered along the way where the Connect dialog could silently run connection code missing required secrets.

## Summary

- Added ggsql code generation to the SQLite and DuckDB drivers, which have native ggsql readers (sqlite:// and duckdb://), and to the ODBC driver family, PostgreSQL, and Redshift, which route through ggsql's ODBC reader (odbc://Driver=...) as a stopgap until ggsql ships native readers for those engines
- Added a ggsql brand icon to the "Connect With" menu
- Fixed a bug in the Connect dialog where a mechanism with only secret parameters (e.g. a pasted connection string) could never produce a code preview at all, and where the "Connect" action could run code silently missing a required secret (like a password) instead of prompting to include it first

## Notes for reviewers

This isn't complete yet -- it's meant to let others start trying the feature. In particular, the PostgreSQL and Redshift drivers guess at an installed ODBC driver name (e.g. PostgreSQL Unicode, Amazon Redshift ODBC Driver (x64)) since those native drivers have no way to discover what's actually installed, unlike the ODBC driver itself. This is documented in code comments as a stopgap to be replaced once ggsql supports native postgres:// and Redshift readers.

Related to #16008.

https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/0d1fba80-239b-45db-8275-107cd3045fcb

## Test plan

- [ ] Connect With ggsql on a SQLite connection, verify the generated code runs in a ggsql console
- [ ] Same for DuckDB
- [ ] Same for a generic ODBC connection (DSN and Driver mechanisms), verify against an installed ODBC driver
- [ ] Same for PostgreSQL and Redshift via their ODBC stopgap, with the appropriate ODBC driver installed and registered in odbcinst.ini
- [ ] Connect With Python/R on a connection whose mechanism is secret-only (e.g. ODBC's Connection String mechanism) and confirm the dialog now opens after confirming Include Secrets, instead of failing silently
- [ ] Click Connect without first clicking Include Secrets on a connection with a password field, confirm the Include Secrets prompt appears before anything runs

title: e2e(redshift): select the User & Password connection mechanism before configuring
description:
Repairs the Redshift data connections e2e suite, which has been failing since #15956.

That PR added AWS IAM as a second connection mechanism for the Redshift driver. Redshift previously exposed only User & Password, so the new-connection flow advanced straight from provider selection to the configure step, and the test relied on that. With two mechanisms the flow now stops at a mechanism-selection step, and the test's next action -- filling the connection inputs -- had nothing to fill.

The fix is a one-line addition to the suite's `beforeAll`: select **User & Password** after picking the Redshift provider, before filling in the host, port, database, user, and password. The stale comment explaining why no mechanism selection was needed is replaced with the call itself; the note about leaving SSL on (which the serverless endpoint requires) is kept.

### Release Notes

#### New Features

- N/A

#### Bug Fixes

- N/A

### Validation Steps

@:web @:win @:connections @:workbench

The Redshift suite needs `REDSHIFT_TEST_HOST` / `REDSHIFT_TEST_USERNAME` / `REDSHIFT_TEST_PASSWORD` and Tailscale access to the private serverless workgroup; it skips itself where those aren't provisioned. On a rig that has them, confirm `test/e2e/tests/data-connections/redshift.test.ts` gets past `beforeAll` and all three tests pass:

npx playwright test test/e2e/tests/data-connections/redshift.test.ts --project e2e-electron

title: Add AWS IAM authorization to the Redshift data connection driver
description:
Adds AWS IAM as a second connection mechanism to the Redshift driver, alongside User & Password. Redshift issues short-lived database credentials to an IAM identity, so this connects with no database password at all.

## How it works Pick **AWS IAM**, paste the endpoint from the AWS console, and give an AWS profile. The driver reads the workgroup (or cluster) name and its region out of the endpoint hostname, so there is nothing to restate: ``` ...redshift-serverless.amazonaws.com ...redshift.amazonaws.com ``` The `.redshift-serverless.` versus `.redshift.` segment also selects the API, so the user is never asked which flavour of Redshift they are on. One mechanism covers both rather than two near-identical entries in the list. | | API | Keyed on | | --- | --- | --- | | Serverless | `redshift-serverless:GetCredentials` | workgroup name | | Provisioned | `redshift:GetClusterCredentials` | cluster identifier + database user | Credentials come from the standard AWS provider chain, which covers the SSO cache, environment variables, and instance or container roles. With IAM Identity Center there are no long-lived access keys, so that chain is the only way in. Parsing is anchored on the `amazonaws` label rather than searching for a `redshift` one, so a private host that merely contains that label (`warehouse.corp.redshift.example.com`) is refused rather than parsed into a bogus region, and a workgroup whose own name is `redshift` does not shadow the service label. ## Two properties of the API that shaped the design **The username is returned, not supplied.** Redshift derives the database user from the federated identity (`IAMR:AWSReservedSSO_PowerUser_` for an Identity Center principal) and hands it back with the password. A dialog that asked for a username and then fetched only a password would connect as the wrong role or fail outright, so the IAM mechanism does not ask for one. Provisioned clusters are the exception: that API takes a database user, and returns it prefixed, so the returned value is what gets used. **Credentials are short-lived.** 900 seconds by default, 3600 at most, which is well inside an ordinary browsing session. Nothing may capture them once at connect time. `RedshiftClient` now resolves credentials immediately before building each pg client, *inside* the connect-retry loop rather than outside it -- a resuming serverless workgroup can take tens of seconds to accept a connection, so a set fetched once up front can expire before the attempt that finally succeeds uses it. Expiry does not look like a dropped socket, so it needs its own recovery path: an invalid-authorization failure (`28000`/`28P01`) discards the cached credentials, re-mints, and retries once. The same failure without a credential provider is not retried, so a genuinely wrong password stays an error. A reconnect whose *mint* fails is also recoverable -- it leaves no pg client behind, and the resulting "client is closed" is neither a socket nor an auth error, so without an explicit retry the connection would stay dead even after the user fixed their session. A deliberate `end()` is never resurrected. ## Error messages Three failures that look alike from the outside are now reported apart, because their remedies have nothing in common: - **Expired session** -- "Your AWS session for profile 'X' has expired. Run `aws sso login --profile X`." - **No credentials found** -- names the AWS Profile field, and that an empty one falls through to the default chain, which needs a `[default]` profile. This is the common case and the old message misdiagnosed it as expiry. - **Redshift rejecting the request** -- names the workgroup or cluster and its region, and does not mention signing in. Ordering matters here: the SDK reports an expired SSO token as a `CredentialsProviderError` too, so the expiry patterns are matched before the error name, or every real expiry would be classified as "missing". One further case is specific to provisioned clusters. With `AutoCreate` off -- the AWS default, and what this driver asks for so connecting never silently creates a database user -- `GetClusterCredentials` *succeeds* for a user that does not exist and the login is what fails. The cause is an AWS-side decision but the symptom is a bare authentication error pointing nowhere useful, so that failure now appends the actual cause. Keying on the SQLSTATE alone is safe because under IAM the password was minted rather than typed, so an authentication failure cannot be a wrong password. ## Generated code Python uses `redshift_connector` with `iam=True` and embeds no credentials, so the snippet stays valid after the live connection's temporary password has expired. R uses `paws` to mint credentials and feeds the returned user and password into `RPostgres`, since RPostgres has no IAM support of its own. Both honor the Use SSL parameter, so generated code cannot contradict the connection it came from. ## Testing **93 passing.** Verified live against a Redshift Serverless workgroup: credentials minted, connected as the returned `IAMR:` user, cross-database browsing working, and the 3600s request honoured at exactly 60 minutes. Everything else is covered without infrastructure. The credential module's only network-touching pieces are its two senders, so those are the injection seam -- tests assert the request that *would* be sent, not just the response that comes back. That is what pins down `AutoCreate: false` and `DurationSeconds: 3600` being on the wire. | Area | Covered | | --- | --- | | Serverless API | request shape, camelCase mapping, expiry fallback, empty response | | Provisioned API | request shape incl. `AutoCreate: false`, PascalCase mapping, returned `IAM:` prefix preferred over the requested user, database-user precondition short-circuiting before AWS | | Provider caching | reuse, forced refresh, expiry margin pinned from both sides, concurrent coalescing, failures not cached | | Expiry recovery | re-mint on reconnect, `28000` and `28P01` forcing a re-mint and one retry, no retry without a provider, recovery from a reconnect whose mint failed, deliberate close staying closed | | Failure messages | expired vs. missing vs. API, with negative assertions both ways | | Endpoint parsing | serverless, provisioned, `amazonaws.com.cn`, case-insensitivity, unknown hosts, private hosts containing a `redshift` label, a workgroup named `redshift`, other AWS services | | Target resolution | inference, embedded-database precedence, database-user requirement, unrecognized host refused | | Code generation | both languages by both flavours, the Use SSL parameter, and the empty-array fallback | | End-to-end wiring | IAM connection reaching pg with minted credentials, `fields` connection never touching AWS, error advice surviving being wrapped | `RedshiftConnection` gained an optional dependencies bag (`pgClientFactory`, `credentialFetcher`) so the whole chain -- config to credential provider to pg client -- runs in tests with only the AWS call and the socket faked. Without it the IAM wiring was unreachable: the existing tests replace `_client` after construction, which skips it. **Not exercised against AWS:** the provisioned path. A real `GetClusterCredentials` round trip, IAM authorization against the `dbuser:/` ARN, and one provisioned handshake need a cluster, and the test account has none -- it is Serverless only. The request and response shapes are enforced by the SDK's TypeScript types on top of the tests above, so what remains unverified is environment configuration rather than code. Also unobserved live is the refresh at the one-hour mark; it is covered by test but no real credential has yet expired under this code. **Known gaps, deliberately out of scope:** `DbGroups` is unsupported, so a user needing group membership at logon cannot get it. `CustomDomainName` is unsupported, and a cluster reached through a custom domain will not match the endpoint parser -- that degrades gracefully, since unrecognized hosts are refused with a message pointing at User & Password. The AWS Profile field is free text; populating it from `~/.aws/config` the way the ODBC driver populates DSNs is the obvious follow-up. ## Dependencies Adds `@aws-sdk/client-redshift`, `@aws-sdk/client-redshift-serverless`, and `@aws-sdk/credential-providers` (all `^3.734.0`, matching the version already used by the `authentication` extension). Together about 12 MB on disk, costing roughly 27 ms and 12 MB of heap at activation. Loading them lazily would drop that to zero for password-only connections; not done here.

title: e2e(memory): send the VS Code version and build commit in the memory payload
description:
### Summary
The nightly memory payload now says which VS Code release a build is based on and which positron commit it was built from, so a step change on the memory charts can be lined up with an upstream merge without digging through workflow logs.

- Reads `version` and `commit` from the build's `product.json`, where the build already stamps them
- Sends them as optional `vscode_version` and `build_commit` at the payload root
- Omitted (not `'unknown'`) when the build did not stamp them, same rule as `ark_version`
- `commit_sha` is unchanged and documented as the harness checkout, not the build
- `payload_version` stays 1; no report or dashboard changes

### QA Notes
No visible effect until the dashboard reads the new fields (follow-up in e2e-test-insights). Either repo can ship first. Covered by `positron-version.vitest.ts` and `publish.vitest.ts`.

title: e2e(memory): attribute the agent SDK runtime to agent_host, not extension_child
description:
### Summary
When the agent host spawns its helper process (the agent SDK runtime), that helper's memory is now counted under `agent_host` instead of `extension_child`.

The helper shows up as `electron-nodejs (index.js)`, and nothing in its name or command line says it belongs to the agent host, so the labeler put it in the catch-all bucket for things extensions spawn. When build 2026.10.0-25 stopped spawning the agent host, the memory chart showed extensions dropping 161 MB even though no extension changed.

- A generic child of `agent_host` is now counted as `agent_host`
- Also matches the SDK's install path (`agent-host/sdk-cache/`) for lanes where process names aren't available
- Process names, totals, and the set of roles are unchanged; no API or dashboard change

### QA Notes
Unit tests only (`npx vitest run test/e2e/utils/memory/`). Nothing visible changes today: current builds don't start the agent host. It takes effect the next time one does, when the ~247 MB will reappear as one `agent_host` step instead of splitting across two bands.

title: Resolve Posit AI Pass sign-in and gateway config from providers.json
description:
Fixes #15881

Posit AI Pass sign-in and the Next Edit Suggestions gateway URL both read a legacy, undeclared `authentication.positai.*` setting (global scope only) with a hardcoded production fallback, so a `positaiLogin`/`baseUrl` override in `~/.posit/ai/providers.json` was silently ignored.

`positOAuthProvider.ts` now resolves `host`/`clientId`/`scope` from the `positai` provider catalog (providers.json + enforced/env, same precedence every other provider gets), falling back to Positron's own production defaults only when the catalog resolves to ai-config's built-in default -- ai-config's default `clientId` ("rstudio-ide") is RStudio's registered OAuth client, not Positron's, so that field can't just be read straight through. `next-edit-suggestions`'s `getGatewayBaseUrl()` now reads the same catalog via a new `getResolvedProviderBaseUrl` export on the `authentication` extension, instead of the orphaned legacy setting.

Not included: the legacy-settings migration gap the issue also flagged (`authentication.positai.*` was never wired into the providers.json migration map). Those settings are undeclared -- no `package.json` contribution ever existed for them, in this extension or the removed `positron-assistant` -- so there's no real population of users with them set to migrate. Fixing it would also mean extending `ai-lib`'s `LEGACY_CONNECTION_ROWS` schema (currently flat `baseUrl`/`customHeaders` only) to handle `positaiLogin`'s nested shape, in a module already marked for deletion once the legacy channels go away.

This fixes things in Positron, but I think this handling should get centralized (outside of positron) as we do the auth refactor.

### Release Notes

#### Bug Fixes

- Fix Posit AI Pass sign-in and code completions ignoring custom Posit AI login/gateway configuration set in `providers.json` (#15881)

### Validation Steps

@:assistant

1. In `~/.posit/ai/providers.json`, customize the positai config block. See the `Posit AI Staging config` 1password entry for config.
2. Sign out of Posit AI Pass if signed in, then sign back in via the provider configuration dialog.
3. Confirm the device-authorization request targets the configured host (check the url in the browser), not `login.posit.cloud`.
4. Set a custom `positai.baseUrl` in the same file and confirm Next Edit Suggestions' gateway requests target it (no override falls back to `https://gateway.posit.ai`) -- if you have log level TRACE, then check the Next Edit Suggestions output channel: search for `[trace] === LLM REQUEST ===`, there should be a log immediately after with `baseURL=<the baseurl you configured>`


Unit test coverage: `extensions/authentication/src/test/positOAuthProvider.test.ts` (`OAuth parameters from providers.json` suite) exercises both the custom-config and unconfigured-fallback paths.

title: First cell in a document isn't always document's language
description:
Fixes #15957

When a Quarto document has no `jupyter:` kernel in its frontmatter, the document's language came from the first cell's fence language, whatever that language was. A document that opens with a mermaid diagram was treated as a mermaid document: the kernel picker offered mermaid, starting it failed with "No mermaid runtime is available", and the Python cells below it were sent to the console instead of the document kernel.

The fallback now picks the first cell whose language can actually host a kernel, meaning some extension provides runtimes for that language. That comes from the `languageRuntimes` contribution in extension metadata, which is read when extensions are scanned, so the answer is known well before extensions activate or interpreters are discovered. A document made only of diagram cells still has no primary language, which is the existing blank-document path.

The same notion of an executable language now backs the multi-cell run filter, which used to ask whether a runtime was registered at that moment. A cell whose language has a provider but no discovered interpreter is now run and reports the usual missing-interpreter error, rather than being dropped from the run in silence.

This also adds `hasLanguageRuntimeProvider` to the runtime startup service, which is where the list of contributed languages already lives.

### Release Notes

#### New Features
- N/A

#### Bug Fixes
- A Quarto document that starts with a diagram cell no longer takes that cell's language as the document language (#15957)

### Validation Steps

@:quarto

1. Create a .qmd file with no `jupyter:` frontmatter, whose first cell is a mermaid diagram followed by a Python cell:

````
```{mermaid}
graph TD; A-->B;
```

```{python}
x = 1
```
````

2. Check the kernel picker: it should offer Python, not mermaid.
3. Run All. The mermaid cell is skipped and the Python cell runs in the document kernel.
4. Add a second Python cell that prints `x` and run it. It should see the value from step 3, confirming both cells share the document kernel instead of going to the console.
