Addresses #1670 and #1693

The Save, Save All Files, Go Back, Go Forward, Show Quick Access, and Folder Commands buttons now have labels.

I made up the labels for "Show Quick Access" and "Folder Commands" whereas the others use the labels of the associated commands.

Also hid the magnifying glass icon from screen readers; it was browsable via VoiceOver and said nothing (and is redundant given it doesn't do anything different than the adjacent Search button).

For the disabled case, set `aria-disabled="true"` when buttons are disabled. This gets announced as "dimmed" by VoiceOver.

title: Implement standard toolbar keyboard model for TopActionBar
description:
Addresses #1669

## Summary

Change the TopActionBar (toolbar) so it has a single tabstop and the arrow keys (left/right/home/end) are used to move focus between the widgets in the toolbar.

This uses the "roving tabindex" approach, where only the currently focused widget has `tabindex=0`, the rest are `tabindex=-1`. Navigation with arrows moves focus to the next/prev item and adjusts the tabindexes accordingly.

This is the [expected keyboard model for toolbars](https://www.w3.org/WAI/ARIA/apg/patterns/toolbar/) (and is how other toolbars in VSCode behave).

## Implementation Details

- Added a `Set<HTMLElement>` to the `positronActionBarState` which holds refs to the toolbar widgets
- Created a custom hook `useRegisterWithActionBar` that components in the toolbar (`actionBarCommandButton`, etc.) use to add themselves to that Set
- Implement keyboard handling in `PositronActionBar` (but only if it's the top-level ActionBar, not the nested one)
- Changed tabindex from 0 to -1 on the PositronTopActionBarPart; we don't want the entire toolbar to get focus when tabbing around, just the buttons within

## Testing Notes

- The first time you Tab or Shift+Tab into the toolbar, focus goes to the first button
- Use left/right arrows to move around (focus will wrap within the toolbar)
- Use Home / End keys to jump to the start/end of the toolbar
- If you leave the toolbar and return later (focus-wise) the last focused element in the toolbar will get focus again

title: aria-expanded and aria-haspopup for menu buttons

Buttons that display a dropdown menu now have `aria-haspopup="menu"`, and will have `aria-expanded="true"` when the menu is opened (and no `aria-expanded` when the menu is closed).

Also tweaked the accessibility tree for the "Show Quick Actions" button (to the right of Search) and the interpreter and folder commands buttons. These no longer get announced as groups by VoiceOver.

title: Move Preview webview when outer pane moves
description:
This change addresses a number of issues that can cause the Preview pane's contents to not draw, or to draw on top of other elements.

The underlying issue is that the webview hosting the Preview doesn't get redrawn when its parent element is moved without changing its size. In this case, `layoutBody` is called again, but because the size doesn't change, we don't trigger a redraw. The fix is to check the position as well, and fire events when it changes. When the position changes, a redraw is triggered.

(Note, this is slightly different than how the Help pane addresses this same issue; this approach made a little more sense for the Preview pane and minimizes redraws for our use case.)

Addresses https://github.com/posit-dev/positron/issues/1311
Addresses https://github.com/posit-dev/positron/issues/1304

title: Coalesce multiple runtime start requests
description:
This change addresses an issue that can occur when a language runtime takes a while to start, and you try to run code while it's starting. In this case the console notices that no runtime is available to execute the code, and it tries to start one -- but fails spectacularly since one is already starting.

The fix is two-fold:

- The primary fix is to create and cache a deferred promise during runtime start. In this way, we can coalesce start requests: any number of requests to start the runtime can arrive and they will all be serviced by a single promise that resolves when startup is complete.
- Also, if for some reason we're asked to start a runtime that is already running, we don't create a user-facing error (just treat it as a successful startup). 

Addresses https://github.com/posit-dev/positron/issues/1355.

title: Handle capping of fetchSize before sending row requests
description:
Addresses #1585  

Javascript and Python gracefully handle slices where the end index exceeds the actual length of the data. Rust however panics and throws an error in the console. This means if we try to fetch 100 rows when there are only 50 left, the frontend is fine with it, Python is fine with it, but R is not. Rather than relying on this language behavior or adding a language specific fix in ark, we can just handle this on the frontend, before sending a request to the backend and before calling `loadDataFragment`.

One thing to note, because we're handling this in `fetchNextDataFragment`, this only is relevant for subsequent batches of data where the rows remaining is less than fetch size (e.g. rows 100-149 where fetch size = 100). This doesn't help if the initial batch of data is already smaller than fetch size (e.g. a 50 row dataset where fetch size = 100). However, this case is already being handled in [Zed](https://github.com/posit-dev/positron/blob/27110c9f193aa0e1cd744824a717ec3027686a8a/extensions/positron-zed/src/positronZedData.ts#L61-L63), [Python](https://github.com/posit-dev/positron-python/blob/f5f5084482a23713689f27c4ed822ca827299536/pythonFiles/positron/dataviewer.py#L50-L52), and [R](https://github.com/posit-dev/amalthea/blob/e4e8601ff78e9e72e0cf67e51278ee8acd313dc2/crates/ark/src/data_viewer/r_data_viewer.rs#L230-L232) by returning early, so we're already covered in that case

title: remove column defs dependency
description:
The column defs contain no data, just a specification for the columns of data that we expect. Because the columns won't change as new rows arrive, there's no need to re-run the hook whenever we receive new rows, as long as we tweak the accessorFn to not rely on data outside of its input params (except for the column index, which again, won't change as more data is received).

Also, the col-number and col-{type} classes were removed even prior to the initial implementation of the data viewer. And it's not so simple to add them back, because we don't have a singular data type "number" across language packs, we allow R and Python to send the type names that are native to their language. So just removing the unused CSS here; eventually we may want to allow for language packs to send both language-specific (ie. float64) as well as generic data types (ie. number, string) that can be shared across languages if we want to display those type categories differently on the frontend, but there's no need for this now

title: fix role for top toolbar
description: Addresses #1668 The top toolbar has `role="appbar"` which isn't a [valid aria role](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/Accessibility/ARIA/Roles). Fixed by changing to `role="toolbar"`. This has a significant impact on the behaviour of assistive tech when navigating to and in the toolbar. In fact, changing the role (or any aria attribute) ONLY impacts the accessibility tree (used by screen readers); so when aria is invalid, it is not noticeable except via screen reader usage and/or tools like Axe and Lighthouse. With this change in place, #1671 becomes a factor; that fix will follow. There are other accessibility problems with this toolbar, and the widgets inside it, which will come in separate fixes.

title: Add basic workspace/runtime affiliation
description:
This change adds a basic form of workspace/runtime affiliation, such that runtimes stick to workspaces: if you start a runtime in a workspace, it will be started for you automatically the next time you open that workspace. 

There's more work to do here; this change is intended to address the minimal set of changes needed for Private Alpha. In this form, it primarily just remembers what you had running and brings it back online. An affiliation can be removed by *manually* shutting down a runtime (using the power button in the toolbar). 

A known issue with this approach is that it doesn't address the case where the affiliated runtime never gets registered (e.g. your project wants R 4.3, but you uninstalled it); the desirable behavior is likely that we should start a different R interpreter, but the behavior in this PR is that we don't start anything. That'll have to wait until after Alpha. 

Addresses https://github.com/rstudio/positron/issues/650.

title: `with_vector!()` macro
description:
The idea is to be call a lambda on a specific `*Vector* class, e.g. 

```rust
with_vector!(value, |v| {
            let formatted = v.format(" ", 100);
            BindingValue::new(formatted.1, formatted.0)
}).unwrap()
```

the macro does the dispatch, so `v` gets to be either a `IntegerVector`, a `NumericVector`,  a `Factor` etc ... 

You get either: 
  - `Ok(<whatever the lambda returns>)`
  - `Err(NotSimpleVectorError)` (part of the `Error` enum)

title: Add JavaScript language runtime and global API accessor
description: This change adds a Javascript-backed language runtime to Positron. It supports basic code execution/evaluation, displays output and errors with tracebacks, and has an Environment pane for variable inspection. It doesn't contain an LSP, but it plays well with VS Code's existing Javascript extension for autocompletion/etc. Currently, the runtime is most useful for inspecting the state of the Extension Host process, either in release builds or in development builds that are detached due to tooling reasons. Run _Javascript: Connect Extension Host Runtime_ to start it. This will give you a _Node.js_ runtime that is connected to the Node extension host process. The JavaScript language runtime should be considered more of a prototype and internal development tool than anything else; it is designed to be used by the Positron development team, not end users. While we could probably reuse much of the code if we were to create a real Javascript language runtime, this one is not production-ready, as it evaluates code directly against the extension host. A real Javascript language runtime would create a dedicated thread, worker, or process to execute the code, but this would make it less useful to the Positron development team. So, until we want to invest in a user-focused Javascript runtime, this one gets buried behind a command. I've also created a global accessor function `acquirePositronApi()` that returns the Positron API; this is part of https://github.com/rstudio/positron/issues/809. What can you do with this? - easily get the extension host process ID for debugging - call the Positron API interactively - check the exact Node version of the extension host - get very detailed Positron build and version information - other fun things that you're already imagining

title: Add support for language-supplied interpreter prompt
description:
This is a small change that makes it possible for a language runtime to specify what input prompt should be used in the Console.

There's a lot it does not do, such as supporting prompt customizations or reacting to changes users make to their prompt strings, but for MVP I think all we need is to look more like a native interpreter by using the same prompt text.

Note that we still need some work to align the prompt text with the input control, and account for the arbitrarily longer prompts which we'll have in the future when we support customization.

title: Save and replay input history
description:
Makes Positron responsible for storing and replaying the input history, so that when you open e.g. a new R console, you can still reference commands you ran in previous R consoles.

After this change, you can write some commands, close Positron, reopen, and press Up in a Console tab to see the commands you ran in your last session.

Note that the command history is stored per user, so it transcends workspaces. 

TODO (before or after merge):

- [x] Remove the history getter parts of the language runtime API -- we could leave these in but practically speaking it probably doesn't make sense to try to merge histories (and most Jupyter kernels don't support the associated messages anyway according to the docs)
- [x] Add a configurable upper bound to the size of the history
- [x] Store execution history entries with a type `<T>` so that we can insert them with stronger types
- [ ] Consider sorting history to ensure commands are never saved out of order (could happen in existing code if you have multiple Positrons open, but also could impact performance)

title: Use background/hidden terminals for Jupyter kernels
description:
This change hides the terminals that the Jupyter Adapter uses to run the R and Python kernels as children of the ptyHost. These terminals generally aren't useful to end users, and it would be confusing to show them. 

Prior to this change, we needed a terminal window to ascertain whether a kernel was running. After it, we don't attempt to interrogate the terminal directly (since it is not API addressable after an extension host reload). Instead, we just check the status of the underlying process ID; if it's running, we try to connect to it.

The old behavior, wherein the terminal still shows up in the Terminal tab, is still accessible for debugging purposes under a new setting, _Positron > Jupyter Adapter > Show Terminal_.

Fixes https://github.com/rstudio/positron/issues/214.

title: [WIP] POC of proxy help server
description: This PR puts together the pieces required to allow Positron to view HTML content from the R help server. The implementation is roughly as follows: 1. The `ark` extension now runs a lightweight proxy server, which simply forwards requests and responses from the R help server. It also ensures that access control is set in a way that allows Positron to fetch and mutate content from that server. 2. The `ark` extension detects attempts to navigate to the R help server, and handles those by instead redirecting to the running proxy server. The proxy server is implemented in Rust, and is built on top of [hyper](https://github.com/hyperium/hyper). `hyper` is used behind the scenes in a number of popular Rust HTTP libraries, e.g. [reqwest](https://crates.io/crates/reqwest). Note that getting this to behave with the existing VSCode content security policies appeared to require using a VSCode webview as opposed to a plain iframe, so some of the existing front-end code managing the Help pane will need to change to accommodate that.

title: Add orchestration for RPC-like treatment of client messages
description:
Even though comms technically can pass any kind of data from either side at any time, in practice most of the communication looks like RPCs. This change adds some orchestration at the runtime level so that it is possible to use RPC idioms to interact with the backend, even though the underlying transport has not changed. 

High level overview:

- When the client sends a message to the server, its message metadata is cached as a pending RPC. It's later paired up with the response when the server emits one.
- The server can now send two distinct kinds of messages to the client: events, which do not have a parent message, and RPC responses, which do. 
- The type system is now used to separate the types that can be used to send data (input) from those that are received from the server (output), and all clients are parameterized over both types.
- The framework exposes a method of calling RPCs wherein strongly typed request data can be passed, yielding a promise that returns the response or an error. 

Note that because we have pending RPC pairs, it is now necessary for RPC-like messages to always have a reply from the server; otherwise, pending RPCs can accumulate unbounded. These responses can take one of three forms in the Environment:

- A reply with a specific type, e.g. `refresh` returns a `list`
- A reply `success` indicating successful execution but no results, e.g. `clear` does not return anything by design
- A reply `error` indicating an error during execution

It is TBD whether we want to try to impose this scheme on all comms we use; for now they apply only to the Environment. 

Unit tests included for the Rust side of this change, where we now ensure that RPC-like messages return responses that identify the request as the parent ID.

title: Add support for kernel-initiated comms
description:
This change adds support for comms that are initiated (and created) by the backend rather than the frontend. Formerly the only way to create a comm was for the frontend to request for one to be created; after the change, either the frontend or backend can create a comm. 

Overview of the changes:

- The `CommSocket` type now contains a pair of channels, `incoming` for messages from the frontend to the backend, and `outgoing` for messages from the backend to the front end.
- A new `CommManager` now owns all of the message routing between comms and other sockets/threads. 
- The `Kernel` interface can now send messages to the comm manager to cause channels to be opened/closed. This interface is available publicly.
- Kernel users (e.g. ARK) can create the exposed `CommSocket` type and send it to the kernel to establish a connection with the front end.

title: Implement back end -> front end comm messages
description:
This change fleshes out a previously unimplemented part of the language runtime framework: specifically, it makes it possible for "comms" (client instances, such as the Environment pane) to send messages to the front end.

It also dramatically simplifies the code needed to implement a comm. Formerly, you had to provide a Rust struct that could be sent across threads (`Send`) and implemented a trait. After this change, the contract just gives you a `Sender<Value>` (where `Value` is any JSON data). Sending data to the channel causes it to be forwarded to the front end.

It works something like this:

```mermaid
graph LR
comm1 -- data --> receiver1 --> select -- metadata --> i[IOPub] -- zeromq --> Positron
comm2 -- data --> receiver2 --> select
comm3 -- data --> receiver3 --> select
```

That is: each comm gets its own unique `Sender` channel which has a unique `Receiver` channel. A dedicated thread runs a `Select` that waits for any of the comms to emit data. When a `Receiver` emits data, we look up the metadata associated with the comm and amend the message with the comm's ID. This gets further wrapped up with Jupyter headers and delivered to the front end via ZeroMQ.

Unit tests are included for the above that test sending data to and receiving data from a comm; the tests use a dummy comm implementation that just echoes any data sent to it. This implementation is also a useful reference for the simplest possible comm.

Finally, this change also adds retry logic to the R Language Pack's server connectivity. For now this is borrowed from the Python Language Pack, but we should have something more robust here (will file an issue).

title: Code-sign and notarize Positron
description:
This change makes four major changes to the Positron release for macOS. Taken together, they will make the experience of downloading, installing, and running Positron about as pleasant as macOS allows for applications downloaded from the Internet. 

### (1) Hardened Runtime

Positron now uses the [Hardened Runtime](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/security/hardened_runtime) in release mode. This mode is more restrictive, but improves security and is a prerequisite to notarization.

Positron requires more runtime entitlements than VS Code does because of the shenanigans we use to load the right version of R, plus capabilities we want R (and other language runtimes) to have when run inside Positron.

### (2) Code-signing

Positron is now code-signed using a Developer ID certificate. As we're still waiting for a Posit branded certificate, the certificate used here is the same one we use to sign builds of RStudio (it's owned by RStudio, PBC). 

### (3) DMG delivery

Positron builds and releases on macOS are now published as disk images (DMG) instead of zip files. The DMG file contains a shortcut to Applications so you can drag Positron to Applications to install it, after the typical macOS fashion.

### (4) Notarization

Notarization allows Positron to run without dire security warnings on macOS, by including a stapled "ticket" from Apple that indicates it was checked for malicious software. Notarization requests must be submitted using an Apple account. As we're still waiting for a Posit Apple service account, the notarization is currently using my personal Apple account, which is what RStudio does.

Four new Github Actions secrets are used:

 - The developer ID certificate (an encrypted .p12 file)
 - The password (or key) used to decrypt the developer ID certificate
 - The name of the Apple account used for notarization
 - The password for the Apple account used for notarization

Addresses https://github.com/rstudio/positron/issues/73
Addresses https://github.com/rstudio/positron/issues/74

This PR takes a [Kool-Aid man busting through a wall](https://youtu.be/_fjEViOF4JE) approach to starting an R runtime while the R extension is activating (specifically, alongside registering the runtimes). In the longer run, we want to think through the proposal @jmcphers made about only starting runtimes from Positron, not from any extensions, but for alpha we don't want folks to have to think about starting what they may think of as default runtimes. This change will start an R runtime even when we have no `.R` files open, no workspace open, no nothing.

To check out the experience:

- stop all your runtimes
- `rm -rf ./.profile-oss`
- start Positron in a factory fresh state

This PR does not address starting any Python runtimes. Perhaps we can add some similar functionality? Or maybe not important for alpha.

title: Add a new message type to separate runtime output from stderr/stdout output
description:
Prior to this change, all output from the language runtime was sent in `Output` messages. This made it impossible to differentiate text generated from standard output, text generated from standard error, and actual output from the language runtime. 

After it, there is a new `Stream` message type that contains stdout/stderr output.

Also, this change fixes an inadvertent deviance from the Jupyter spec; the field containing the name of the output stream is `name`, not `stream`. A few `rustfmt` changes result.

title: Add support for static plots
description: Adds support for showing static plots in Positron. "Static" here just means plots that don't know how to render themselves and can only be shown at one size. This change works by reading any plot (defined as "an output with a `image/` mimetype") emitted by a kernel and adding it to the Plots pane, so it works as-is with the IPyKernel and any other compliant Jupyter kernel.

title: Add new "Statement Range Provider" to power "Execute Current Statement"
description:
This change adds a whole bunch of plumbing that makes it possible for language packs to provide intelligent statement range detection -- that is, finding the current statement around the cursor point. These are subsequently used by the Execute Statement command (Cmd+Enter). Here's a video of the feature in action:

https://github.com/posit-dev/positron/assets/470418/0463d3de-a91e-4e82-979f-016b702b8f5f

The API is modeled after VS Code's [programmatic language features](https://code.visualstudio.com/api/language-extensions/programmatic-language-features) system. Any extension can supply a `StatementRangeProvider`, which is just a function that accepts a `Position`, indicating the user's cursor point, and returns a `Range`, indicating the statement to execute. 

When the user presses Cmd+Enter, we use a `StatementRangeProvider` (if one is registered) to determine the boundary of the current statement, then use it again to find the boundary of the next statement. This makes it possible to Cmd+Enter your way through a file, statement by statement.

Note that this PR does not have any effect on its own since it doesn't contain any range providers. I have implemented a simple range provider for Python as a proof of concept (it's demo'ed above and I'll submit a PR for it on the Python repository). 

Part of https://github.com/posit-dev/positron/issues/394.

title: Require Rust 1.64 (for std::ffi)
description:
I was hitting this compile error:

```
error[E0412]: cannot find type `c_char` in this scope
   --> crates/ark/src/interface.rs:212:47
    |
212 |   pub extern "C" fn r_write_console(buf: *const c_char, _buflen: i32, otype: i32) {
    |                                                 ^^^^^^
    |
```

It turned out to be caused by my toolchain; I was using Rust 1.63, but `std::ffi` was introduced in Rust 1.64, and we depend on `c_char` being in `std::ffi` as of this change: https://github.com/rstudio/positron/commit/9345da2c6819b7880bb1c819e8a147f5039643d1

This change makes our dependency on Rust 1.64 formal by adding `rust-version` to our Cargo packages as documented here:

https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/manifest.html#the-rust-version-field

title: End-to-end handling of runtime startup failures
description: This change improves the handling of runtime startup failures. Previously, a runtime that failed to start would appear (to the UI) to just get stuck in the `starting` state, never completing startup. No output or errors were visible to the user. After the change, an explanation of the startup failure appears in the UI. Here's how it is done: - A wrapper script captures all the output of the Jupyter Kernels as they start up. - Inside the Jupyter Kernel adapter, all codepaths that could fail during startup emit a rich error object when they fail. This object includes the output of the kernel during startup as captured by the wrapper. - Various codepaths that didn't propagate errors correctly have been fixed up, and timeouts have been added to ensure that no part of startup is capable of waiting forever. - There is a new event emitter on the Positron side for language runtimes that, `onDidEncounterStartupFailure`. This event fires when a runtime fails to start up. It is fired after the runtime exits to let the UI know that the runtime exited due a startup failure. Fixes https://github.com/rstudio/positron/issues/307.

title: Add 'source' field to runtime metadata

title: Enable language runtime persistence & reconnection after extension host reload/restart
description:
This change moves the language runtimes to their final resting place: they are now children of the "ptyhost" process used by VS Code's internals to host terminal processes across front-end restarts and reconnects. This enables language runtime processes to persist across UI and browser reloads.

The change is somewhat large since we now must account for reconnecting to a language runtime in addition to starting one, and the "create a new runtime" and "connect to it" steps have been factored into separate routines.

The startup sequence now looks something like this. Almost every step is asynchronous.

1. A request is received to start the runtime.
2. Available ports are allocated and a connection file is created.
3. A new terminal process is created to host the runtime. We wait for the terminal to open before proceeding.
4. The name and location of the connection file and the terminal's process ID are saved to workspace storage, under the runtime's ID.
5. We connect all the ZeroMQ sockets and wait for the kernel to deliver a live heartbeat. 
6. When the runtime signals that it's ready, the LSP is started. For this change, I (again) needed to reverse the client/server LSP roles.

After a restart, we do this:

1. When the runtime is registered, we look in workspace storage to see if there's information about a running instance of the runtime.
2. If there is, we check all open terminals to see if there's one whose process ID matches the stored process ID.
3. If we find a match, we attempt to connect to the running terminal, essentially starting at step 5 above.

title: Clarify and lightly refactor runtime metadata
description:
The intent of this change is to clarify the meaning of the fields in the runtime metadata, and to make their use more consistent. Specifically:

- No more bare field names like `id` or `name` -- each field now has more verbose naming (`runtimeId`, `languageName`, etc.)
- The metadata has been augmented with additional fields to reduce confusion and cross-referencing.
- The language runtimes are now responsible for supplying both language ID and language name; this way we avoid confusion about what `language` is, and we also avoid having to guess name from ID or the other way around. IDs are publicly documented here so shouldn't be a huge burden:  https://code.visualstudio.com/docs/languages/identifiers#_known-language-identifiers

title: Add runtime discovery phase; start R eagerly for RStudio users
description:
This change rearranges and improves much of the startup sequencing around language runtime discovery and initialization, with the goal of making it faster and more predictable. These changes also allow us to reliably start the default R for RStudio users of Positron who wouldn't otherwise have a language runtime active.

The core of this change is a refactoring of the language runtime registration system. It adds a new concept to the API, a `LanguageRuntimeProvider`, which asynchronously emits language runtime registrations until it has registered all of them. This enables us to know when runtime registration has started and when it has ended, enabling a number of new behaviors and features.

Here's how things work after the change:

### Step 1: Startup

For performance reasons, we want language runtimes to be registered very early at startup.

Language pack extensions activate eagerly now (`*` instead of `onStartupFinished`). When activating, each one registers a `LanguageRuntimeProvider` . 

Note that no actual runtime discovery or registration happens in this stage, so startup impact is minimal. The language pack is just supplying a callback to be invoked later, in the discovery state.
### Step 2: Startup Complete

When startup is complete, a new event `whenAllExtensionHostsStarted` is emitted. This event indicates that the extension host is started and that all `*` extensions are activated. Thus it means that all `LanguageRuntimeProviders` we need are present and accounted for.

(Note: this part of the change isn't my favorite; it seems like there should already be a way for the main thread to know that extensions are online. However, the `Promise` that tracks this important information is just getting discarded, so I added some goo to save and track it.)
### Step 3: Discovery

The Language Runtime Service emits an event indicating to the UI that it has started discovering runtimes. In the future, we can use this event to show progress UI.

Positron invokes all of the `LanguageRuntimeProviders` and registers each runtime as it is returned from the provider.

If a provider wants a runtime to start up automatically in the workspace, it marks the runtime's metadata with a new  `startupBehavior`, called `Immediate`. This is how the R language pack recommends an R version to start if it finds RStudio state on the machine. 

### Step 4: Discovery Complete

When all of the providers are finished, Positron emits an event indicating to the UI that all runtimes have been discovered. In the future, we can use this event to turn off progress UI.

### Step 5: Auto-Start

If Positron finds that no runtimes have been started, or are scheduled to start, for the current workspace, it looks for a runtime with a `startupBehavior` of `Immediate`. If it finds one, it starts that runtime automatically. 

>[!note]
>As part of this change, I also refactored the R runtimes so that they don't eagerly activate the Jupyter Adapter extension. Instead, they are registered without a Jupyter kernel backing them; we only create the kernel if the user actually starts R. It's slightly more annoying, but it makes registration much more efficient. 

>[!note]
>I did not do the work to make the Python extension to use the new mechanism (that work is tracked in https://github.com/rstudio/positron/issues/1009). This change won't impact Python at all for now, but in order to provider future Python startup improvements (like having the extension tell Positron which Python to start automatically), we will need to update the Python extension to use this new registration mechanism.

>[!warning]
>Github's new support for callouts is nifty, but they are very easy to abuse and tempting to use for paragraphs of text that do not actually warrant a callout.

Supersedes https://github.com/rstudio/positron/pull/937
Addresses https://github.com/rstudio/positron/issues/792

title: Workflow for reviving macOS agent
description:
Adds a new hourly workflow that attempts to revive the macOS build agent. The workflow checks to see if `screen` is running; if it isn't, it starts a new `screen` session, inside which it runs the Github Actions client.

You can see what's going on in the agent (its stdout/stderr logs) by connecting to the host directly and running `screen -r`.

title: Allow 'restart' to work on exited runtimes
description:
If you use the Restart keyboard shortcut after a runtime exits, it doesn't do anything. _Technically_ you can't restart something that isn't running, but I agree with @lionel- in #1038:

> After a crash the user can't restart the runtime with the keybinding which is surprising. 

So, this change implements a more sophisticated restart heuristic which allows the restart command to be smarter about which runtime it acts on, and also allows it to "restart" a runtime that has exited. 

Part of https://github.com/rstudio/positron/issues/1038.

title: Add a keybinding for Restart command
description:
Adds <kbd>Cmd</kbd> <kbd>Shift</kbd> <kbd>0</kbd> as the keybinding for the Restart command.

Also updates the Interrupt, Shutdown and Restart commands so that they don't prompt you to pick a language runtime -- they just use whichever is active. If the user wants to act on a specific runtime instead of the active one, they can use our snazzy new interpreter control center in the top right!

Addresses https://github.com/rstudio/positron/issues/618.

title: R environment pane: named list expansion
description: This is very minimal and limited so far, i.e. only lists can be expanded (this includes data.frames), but at least this wires things for Inspect and Details messages. ```r x <- list(abc = 1:100, list(ghi = letters, iris)) ```

title: enable code signing for Positron builds on macOS
description:
This PR adds the changes necessary for us to be able to sign Positron with our own signing identity, and also makes it possible to sign Positron with an ad-hoc signature (which allows us to test the application with a hardened runtime locally).

With this PR, I can produce a hardened-runtime build of Positron locally, and so far everything Just Works:

```
$ codesign --display --verbose Positron.app
Executable=/Users/kevin/VSCode-darwin-arm64/Positron.app/Contents/MacOS/Electron
Identifier=com.rstudio.positron
Format=app bundle with Mach-O thin (arm64)
CodeDirectory v=20500 size=757 flags=0x10002(adhoc,runtime) hashes=13+7 location=embedded
Signature=adhoc
Info.plist entries=35
TeamIdentifier=not set
Runtime Version=12.3.0
Sealed Resources version=2 rules=13 files=9867
Internal requirements count=0 size=12
```

TODO:

- Import certificate to build host and use it; needs to be placed in `$TMPDIR/buildagent.keychain` IIUC.
- Validate application entitlements are compatible with our own requirements.

title: Separate Positron API
description:
This change separates Positron's API from VS Code's API, with the goal of:

- providing a surface on which to build the next set of APIs we need for e.g. Positron pane usage and UI injection
- reducing merge conflicts from upstream
- keeping VS Code's API untouched in Positron (for extension compatibility)
- allowing extensions to use distinct sets of behaviors in Positron / VS Code based on availability (we are still missing some pieces for bimodal extensions, but this work is necessary first)
- eventually, publishing our API for third party extension authors to write against

The existing Ark and Jupyter Adapter extensions have been updated to use the Positron API in addition to the VS Code API; there's also some plumbing changes necessary to create a separate API factory instance and load it as a module when extensions need it.

title: scaffolding for Plots pane
description: Not actually functional yet. Mostly just copied from the existing Environment pane and renamed a few things.

title: Connect Positron plots to plot service
description: This change adds some middleware that wraps Positron plots in a UI-friendly object for rendering and storing in history. The new object is a `PlotClientInstance`, and it can supply a plot rendering of any dimensions by requesting the same from the back end. Most of the change is the UI plumbing required for these objects to be constructed at the right time and attached to the right place in the UI. As a proof of concept, this change also adds a dynamic (resizable) plot to the Zed `plot` command. The Zed "plot" is rendered as an SVG that shows its own requested dimensions along with a test pattern.

title: Plot history, part 2
description:
This is the next iteration of plot history changes. It does the following:

- Makes the plot history thumbnail gallery scrollable
- Aligns the plot history thumbnail gallery along the shortest edge of the Plots pane instead of always sticking it at the bottom
- Records plot metadata and uses it to correctly sort plots when reconnecting to a runtime and replaying its plot history

It is this last item that requires the most work; because the runtime itself can only tell us the IDs of the plots it knows about on reconnect, we don't have any idea what their correct ordering is. We address this by saving each plot's metadata when it is first emitted, and then checking the storage service for this metadata when the runtime reconnects.

title: Correctly compute enabled state for each toolbar item in the Plots pane
description: Computes the enabled state on each toolbar item in the Plots pane, to make it clear which are applicable to the current state. Fixes an uncaught exception that occurs when attempting to clear the plot when there's no plot active.

title: Plots: actions bar and more
description: A bunch of improvements to the Plots pane, including: - better UX for history view - a new Actions bar with Previous, Next, Delete Current, and Delete All buttons - full keyboard accessibility; history items now have focus targets and can be navigate, selected, and deleted with the keyboard

title: Process plot updates on the front end
description: Adds support for the `update` message, which is a notification from the server that the plot has changed and needs to be redrawn. Companion to https://github.com/posit-dev/amalthea/pull/73.

title: Improve sizing and display heuristics in Plots pane; add user-controllable policies
description: This change adds some new tools to the Plots pane and changes some of its heuristics, making the default sizing behavior better and adding some options for controlling it. ## Sizing Policy The first part of the change adds a sizing policy chooser to the Plots pane (yes, we'll need a better icon than a ruler). The sizes are pretty self-explanatory; _Fill_ corresponds to the current Positron behavior (and RStudio behavior). The new default, _Auto_, is similar to _Fill_, but adds constraints: - The plot won't shrink smaller than 400px. If the pane is smaller than 400px, the plot is still drawn at 400px and then scaled to the pane. - The plot's aspect ratio will not exceed the Golden Ratio (in either direction). If it does, a Golden Ratio plot will be drawn instead and then centered in the pane. There's also a _Custom_ sizing policy, which lets you pick whatever (fixed) size you want. ## History Policy The second part adds a history policy chooser. This just lets you decide whether you'd like Positron to show the history panel (filmstrip) always, never, or automatically. The automatic behavior has been improved as follows: - The heuristics for placing the history on the right or bottom have been adjusted to prefer wide plots to tall ones, since these are more common in publications. - If the plots pane is very small, we won't show the history panel at all. Addresses https://github.com/posit-dev/positron/issues/462 Addresses https://github.com/posit-dev/positron/issues/940

title: Navigable plot history in Plots pane
description: Adds a very basic, unstyled plot history view to Positron. The plot history view shows the most recently emitted plots and lets you re-examine any previously emitted plots. It aggregates the plots emitted by all the language runtimes, so you may see a mix of Python, R, and Zed plots, both static (i.e. plain PNG or SVG) and dynamic (resizable/redrawable) plots.

title: Add basic support for persisted plot history
description:
This change causes Positron to preserve plot history when reloading the browser. It works by asking each runtime, as we connect to it, to list all the active plot widgets. Each is then emitted to the Plots pane as a "new" plot.

Almost all the change exists at the level of the comm infrastructure; prior to this change, the plumbing to list open comms was not fully connected. Now it is! I have also implemented (and added unit tests for) the filter-by-target-name feature required by the Jupyter spec. 

I'd like to get it merged soon so we can build on top of it, but there are known limitations:

- Only plots backed by an active language runtime are preserved. Static plots are lost on reload, since they (currently) exist only in browser memory.
- The plots are not guaranteed to be ordered in the same way after reload. This ordering information will need to be saved somewhere, probably in the storage service or in a context key.  
- Thumbnails for plots other than the most recent one are blank until clicked. We probably want to load these very lazily so we don't overwhelm the runtime with render demands right after connecting to it.

title: Don't restore .RData workspaces; add option for command-line arguments
description: This change adds a couple of new settings. The first causes Positron to default to _not_ loading `.Rdata` by default, by passing `--no-restore-data` to R in the default argument list. The second provides a way to pass arbitrary command line arguments to R. It's not likely to be used by average R users, but can be helpful for developers. For example, you can make R emit a lot of verbose output by adding `--verbose` as an extra argument. Note that this PR also bumps the Amalthea submodule to pick up the required kernel changes to support this work (see https://github.com/posit-dev/amalthea/pull/70). Addresses https://github.com/rstudio/positron/issues/930.

title: R environment pane, value for vectors
description: wip, but this improves the situation for lgl, int, dbl, raw and str vectors and arrays: ```r x <- rnorm(20) y <- matrix(20, ncol = 4) y <- matrix(1:20, ncol = 4) z <- letters Z <- matrix(LETTERS[1:4], ncol = 2) a <- 1:10 > 5 # not great, maybe should show TRUE and FALSE instead ```

title: Include timestamps on all language runtime messages
description: This change adds ISO 8601 timestamps in a new `when` field on all language runtime messages. It's pretty small since this information was already being recorded; it was just being discarded before the message crossed the extension host boundary.

title: Create universal build artifacts from the main branch
description: On the `main` branch, the macOS universal binary currently is published as a release instead of (not in addition to) a build artifact. This has proven somewhat confusing, as some builds have universal build artifacts and some don't. This change causes all builds, even those from `main`, to produce a build artifact with a universal binary.

title: Reconnect LSP on reload
description:
This change makes it possible to reload the Positron front end/window/browser tab and have a working LSP afterwards. This is useful both for iterative development on the front end and for browser-based session resumption.

Prior to this change, the LSP only ever started once, and we specified its port ahead of time with the rest of the network ports needed for the kernel.

After this change, a new LSP client/server pair is created every time Positron connects to the kernel. The creation of the LSP backend is triggered by a message that opens a custom comm; for accounting purposes, the LSP looks to the kernel like a client widget (which, if you squint, it kind of is).

title: Handle reconnect in Jupyter Adapter
description:
This change makes it possible for a Jupyter kernel to be marked offline and then come back online if it begins responding to heartbeats again, or emits any other message.

Fixes https://github.com/rstudio/positron/issues/583.

title: Add execution history service
description: Adds an execution history service, which listens to input and output from language runtimes and saves it to durable storage for later replay.

title: support automatic generation of event interfaces
Update labels in Environment and Console when runtime changes
description: This addresses an issue in which the Environment and Console panes can show the wrong versions of a language when you switch versions inside a Positron session, as described here: https://github.com/posit-dev/positron/pull/1154#issuecomment-1693316855

title: Add tests for environment pane
description:
This change adds integration tests for the new environment pane. The test starts R, verifies that an initially empty environment is delivered, adds a variable, refreshes the environment, and verifies that the variable shows up. It uses a `Sender`/`Receiver` pair to simulate those operations being performed by the front end. 

Note that because the environment pane is an independent module, the tests can run outside the context of the R kernel and Amalthea. 

Also note that since tests don't get access to `main` modules (only `lib` modules) I've split `ark` into main/lib pieces.

title: Update protocol messages for environment pane
description:
Adds new types and metadata to environment messages. 

Also adds a new Zed command to make it easier to test the UI for truncated environment limits, `env max 100` tells Zed to only show 100 variables in the environment (while still telling the UI the total number available).

title: Front end and Zed support for new environment pane messages
description:
This change does four things:

1. Adds client (Positron) side typing and support for new types and messages used by the nascent Environment pane protocol
2. Adds two new commands to Zed that update and remove variables from the environment (`update X` and `rm X`)
3. Makes the Environment UI respond correctly to the new message types
4. Adds a wrapper around the Environment server communicator/client instance that emits strongly typed messages

title: Implement basic environment pane structure
description:
This change contains a very simple but functional environment pane implementation for R. It has the following features:

- Lists the initial environment when the environment pane is shown
- Shows the names of all of the variables in the global environment
- For variables containing string data, shows the value of each variable
- Refreshes the environment list from R when the refresh button is pressed

The underlying transport is a symmetric interface (a "comm channel") over which the front end and back end can send any kind of data they like. Currently there are only 3 messages that can be sent:

- `refresh`, a message that requests new data from the back end
- `list`, a message that delivers a fresh set of environment data to the front end. It is sent both when the pane is first created and in response to a refresh request. 
- `error`, a message indicating an error on the back end

The main work from here is:

- Adding rich JSON representations for each type of object that can be encountered in the environment, along with appropriate visualizations for those objects in the pane
- Adding incremental synchronization; delivering additional messages when variables or values have changed so they can be updated in the UI
- Implementing a Python backend

title: Add plumbing for client widgets (environment pane, etc)
description: This PR adds the necessary plumbing to create clients (widgets) on the front end that talk to stateful objects on the back end.

title: Add middleware for object inspection
description: This change adds some middleware for handling object inspection (so far, just expanding/collapsing children) in Positron. The major changes are as follows: - We now support the `inspect` (request) and `detail` (response) message types. - The raw `IEnvironmentClientMessage*` types for lists, updates, and variables, are no longer exposed to the front end. Instead, we use wrapper `EnvironmentClient*` types that add the additional metadata need to make and respond to inspection requests. - The Zed language now has a `list` type that can contain other kinds of Zed variables, including lists. You can click on `(+)` to query for the children of a List, and it will retrieve them from Zed, but I did not attempt to do any rendering of the results (will leave that up to @softwarenerd)

title: Use access keys to inspect variables
description: Instead of passing `display_name` as the path, use `access_key` to access child/sub-variables.

title: Use DYLD_FALLBACK_LIBRARY_PATH workaround for SIP
description: Uses an alternate variable name to workaround macOS SIP policy that prevents this value from being inherited as we need it to for R.

title: Debounce plot render requests
description:
This change improves the responsiveness of the Plots pane, especially when it contains plots that take a long time to draw. Specifically:

- Render requests are now debounced, so we only issue them after the user has stopped changing the size of the plot pane for a set period of time (currently 500ms). This dramatically speeds up perceived performance since it effectively gets rid of the stacked render queue.
- When a plot is waiting to be re-rendered, it is now shown at its natural aspect ratio in the way that best fits the plot window, instead of being stretched.
- During a render operation, we now show a progress bar to make it clear that we are doing work. If the plot has been previously rendered and is now being re-rendered, we use the plot's previous render time to approximate the progress towards the next render. 

Fixes https://github.com/rstudio/positron/issues/359.

title: Use TanStack table in data viewer
description:
This change switches the data viewer from a simple HTML table to a much more robust viewer with better styling and fixed headers, built on TanStack. 

It also adds very basic virtualization to the table using TanStack's react-query and react-virtual packages. This virtualization is DOM-only; the data is still all loaded at once. A future PR will load the data incrementally from the backend.

title: Initial work on Data Viewer
description: This change adds an extremely basic data viewer to Positron. The data viewer renders a simple HTML table showing a fixed data set. The data viewer is implemented as a built-in extension. It's a somewhat large change, so here are the broad strokes: - There are two new extensions, `positron-data-viewer` and `positron-data-viewer-ui`. - `positron-data-viewer` is the orchestrator. It listens for viewable data (defined as "a comm of type `positron.dataViewer`") to be emitted by language runtimes. It opens a editor tab for each one and feeds it data from the comm. - `positron-data-viewer-ui` contains a standalone React webapp that runs in a Webview in the editor tab. When the app opens, it emits a `ready` message, then loads the data sent to it via a `data` message. - There's a new field for variables in Environments, `has_viewer`, and a new message, `view`. Variables that set `has_viewer: true` get a new _View_ context entry in the Environment pane; invoking this sends the new `view` message to the runtime. It's up to the runtime to decide what it means to "view" an object. - The Zed language runtime contains a sample implementation of the data viewer backend. You can cause it to emit a data viewer by running the `view` command, or by invoking the context menu on a Zed table object and clicking on View.

title: hacky PR for checking if suggest widget is visible
description:
Surely there is a better way... see comments in PR for details.

Closes https://github.com/rstudio/positron/issues/338.

title: Add support for basic HTML outputs
description: This change adds support for basic HTML output from language runtimes. The primary intent of the change is to allow us to render HTML pretty-printed output from e.g. `pandas` in the Positron console. This was pretty difficult in the end due to security constraints, which prevent us from using any of the usual browser APIs to load HTML from the kernel (e.g. `innerHTML`, `DOMParser`), and packaging constraints, which prevent us from using any of the popular battle-tested HTML parsing libraries (e.g. `parse5`). We will need to revisit this later, because this scheme doesn't work for richer content. My hope is that we can continue to display simpler HTML in the console (for performance reasons), upgrading to an iframe or a wholly different Positron pane (plots?) for more interactive content. Adding support for HTML output also opens up some interesting possibilities for our R kernel, which currently only returns text. Addresses https://github.com/rstudio/positron/issues/928.

title: Enable REnvironment to run against any environment; refine tests
description:
Prior to this change, we always hooked up the environment monitor/listing service to the R global environment. 

After it, you need to specify which environment to attach to. This is useful:

- in the tests, so that the tests can run on clean, isolated environments (will be a requirement to allow environment tests to run in parallel without seeing each others' data), and
- eventually in Positron, as a way to get a live view into other environments (for debugging, drilling into nested envs, etc.)

title: name threads spawned in amalthea
description: This PR makes life easier when debugging crashes in Ark, as the debugger can now show thread names. For example, the one I'm investigating now: With this PR, we can clearly see the faulting thread is 'ark-shell'.

title: Move amalthea/ark to a submodule
description: Addresses #524

title: Move Amalthea/ARK to a git submodule
description: Addresses https://github.com/rstudio/positron/issues/524.

title: add boost::signals-like Signal class
description:
See tests for example usage. The general idea is you can declare a struct full of signals, e.g. something like:

```
struct Signals {
    console_prompt: Signal<String>
}

static SIGNALS: Signals = Signals::new();  // or the 'Lazy::new()' equivalent
```

and then use `SIGNALS.listen()` to attach a handler, and `SIGNALS.emit()` to emit data.

We might want to iterate on the interface depending on how this actually feels with e..g Rust object lifetimes but I think this is a nice start, and it felt better having our own implementation that serves our own needs.

title: use macro to generate event types
description: @jmcphers, let me know if you think this is worthwhile or if you prefer being explicit.

title: R environment pane handling `::Clear` and `::Delete` messages
handle CharacterVector::create(Vec<String>)
description: allow `CharacterVector::create(Vec<String>)` by bringing back some traits and implementation from before #305, so that we don't have to first convert a `Vec<String>` into a `Vec<&str>` as I'm struggling with in #310.

title: Environment.iter()
keep 'Attach to VS Code' launch target around
description: Required for debugging of tests.

title: Include github user with PAT
description: This change is intended to address an issue causing builds to hang waiting for a password on the macOS build instance.

title: Avoid driving focus to console on interpreter restart
description:
This fixes an issue in which restarting an interpreter drives focus to the console.

It turned out that focus was being driven to the console because the interpreter, after becoming ready again, is re-selected as the active interpreter. That's the moral equivalent of clicking the interpreter in the top bar interpreter dropdown (which _does_ drive focus to the console, even if it is the current interpreter). 

The fix is pretty simple: we don't fire runtime activation events when the runtime becomes ready but is already the active runtime.

Addresses https://github.com/rstudio/positron/issues/927.

title: Store discovery phase completion status in extension host
description:
This change addresses another timing issue that contributes to #1003. In particular, using the main thread as the source of truth about whether discovery is complete was causing a race condition in which we were getting a stale value back. 

The fix is to track whether or not discovery is complete inside the extension host so we don't need an asynchronous trip to the main thread to check it.

title: Allow for provider registration during discovery
description:
This change fixes an issue spotted by @seeM, in which there is a brief window of time (during Discovery) when injecting a new runtime provider results in that provider never getting invoked to register runtimes. 

The fix is to check the set of runtime providers before and after discovery; if it's changed, we perform another discovery pass on the new providers before considering the discovery phase complete. 

Part of #1003.

title: Show runtime version in console
description: Like this: Addresses https://github.com/rstudio/positron/issues/983.

title: Eliminate `connect_delay` log spam
description:
This change addresses an issue in which a bad 0MQ state can lead to the Output logs filling up with `socket failed to connect` errors. In this state, a connected socket begins to emit `connect_delay` events rapidly. The fix for the problem is to:

- stop monitoring the socket for events once we have determined it to be in a failed/timed out state, and
- ignore connection delays once we have successfully connected (i.e. we have settled the connection promise successfully)

This change doesn't fix the underlying 0MQ issue that causes the socket to get into this state (we don't have a bead on that yet); it only causes us to treat that state more sanely by preventing it from generating lots of logs and repeated rejections of an already-settled promise. 

Partially addresses https://github.com/rstudio/positron/issues/746.

title: Speculative fix for intermittent comm_id unit test failure
description:
This change is a speculative fix for the intermittent following unit test failure:

```
---- test_kernel stdout ----
thread 'test_kernel' panicked at 'assertion failed: comms.contains_key(comm_id)', crates/amalthea/tests/client.rs:317:13
```

This fix is to implement busy/idle wrappers around the shell messages that handle comm open/comm message handling. This is what they are supposed to do anyway (as per the kernel spec), and emitting these/handling them gives the system time to reconcile the state.

title: Aways clean session state when connection fails
description: Ensure that, when reconnection fails, we always clean the session state so we don't try to reconnect again.

title: Do not disconnect background terminals on reload
description:
Positron uses background (hidden) terminals to run the R and Python kernels. Unfortunately, a recent upstream change to VS Code causes background terminals to be destroyed 1 minute after a window reload, so reloading Positron now effectively kills all your R and Python sessions. 

It is my view that the upstream behavior is a bug, but we probably don't want to wait for Microsoft to address it, so I'm adding this small patch to address our use case so we stay unblocked. 

The fix here is to avoid calling `detachProcessAndDispose` on background terminal instances when reloading the window. That call is meant to _temporarily_ detach a terminal, but for a background terminal instance, it has the effect of _permanently_ detaching the terminal, since background terminals aren't saved to the `TerminalGroupService`. The `PtyHost` times out waiting for the terminal to reattach and, after a minute of waiting, sends it a `SIGHUP`, killing it. 

Addresses https://github.com/rstudio/positron/issues/939.

title: use atomic integer rather than flag to coordinate access to R runtime
description: Closes https://github.com/rstudio/positron/issues/255.

title: ensure interrupt handler is reset appropriately
description:
As learned with @jmcphers, R tries to temporarily install its own interrupt signal handler when select is invoked, e.g. here:

https://github.com/wch/r-source/blob/e7a21904029917a63b4717b53a173b01eeabcc7b/src/unix/sys-std.c#L171-L179

However, something about the way that R tries to save and restore the signal handler seems to cause issues -- when the interrupt is handled, it can get executed on the wrong thread (e.g. the "main" thread instead of the thread actually hosting R).

This PR tries to side-step the issue by making sure to reinstall the interrupt handler whenever R_Busy is invoked (which it seemingly is after an interrupt is handled).

Closes https://github.com/rstudio/positron/issues/291.

title: use debug builds by default; override in CI
Fix build breaks on amd64 and older R
description:
Addresses to build breaks when building Amalthea against amd64 on Linux with older R:

- use system character type instead of `u8` / `i8`
- don't use `R_existsVarInFrame` (it's too new)

Also has a rustfmt pass.

title: Fix data transposition in data viewer
description: This change addresses an issue in which data in the Data Viewer is incorrectly transposed.

title: Ensure kernels are shut down during deactivate
description:
This fixes an issue in which the `ark` kernel does not get cleaned up when Positron exits. It turns out that the main reason for this problem is a simple ordering error: we tear down all of the sockets and then tell the kernel to shut down. However ... the shutdown request is sent over a socket, so it's never delivered! 

The fix is just to tell the kernel to shut down _before_ tearing down the ZeroMQ sockets.

(Note -- changes to spawn options are just to clarify intent.)

title: Fix reconnect regression
description:
This small change addresses https://github.com/rstudio/positron/issues/901.

The issue turned out to be that we mark the kernel as `Exited` when the terminal in which it is running closes. Marking it as Exited causes the session to be cleaned up, so we can't connect to it again even though it's still running.

However, it turns out that VS Code's infrastructure fires close events for terminals when Positron is reloaded, so closing the terminal does not imply the kernel has exited. The kernel is still running and attached to the ptyhost.

The fix is to only mark the kernel `Exited` if there's an actual exit code/status, indicating that the process ended.

title: Implement restart for R
description: This change addresses a number of connected issues with lifecycle management that made it necessary to restart Positron in order to restart R. After the change, the "restart" command works correctly and can be used to hot-reload ARK changes into Positron. The major changes are: - **Jupyter Kernel Wrapper**: R's shutdown was not sequenced correctly because the Jupyter Adapter did not provide the right lifecycle hooks. Rather than add additional lifecycle hooks, however, I've chosen to refactor the way extensions use the Jupyter Adapter. Language packs now create their own Language Runtimes which neatly wrap the Jupyter Adapter's Language Runtime. This proxying layer gives them the flexibility to perform their own custom work and sequencing. Now the R Language Pack can cleanly shut down its LSP client before the kernel itself is shut down, which makes shutdown work gracefully. - **New Restarting State**: Language runtimes now have a `Restarting` state, which is used to distinguish the "exiting because of shutdown" state transition from the "exiting because of restart" transition. Restarting a kernel causes it to go through an otherwise normal set of shutdown and startup events as documented in updates to the state diagram: https://connect.rstudioservices.com/positron-wiki/runtime-state-diagram.html - **Simplified API**: The `adaptKernel` function has gotten an overhaul aided by the refactor to use the wrapper/containment paradigm; it no longer requires twenty arguments, and the entire Jupyter Adapter API is now typesafe using the unfortunately-standard mechanism of copying `.d.ts` files between peer extensions. Note that restart does not work for Python yet. Addresses https://github.com/rstudio/positron/issues/384 Addresses https://github.com/rstudio/positron/issues/581 Addresses https://github.com/rstudio/positron/issues/590 (R only) Must be coordinated with https://github.com/posit-dev/positron-python/pull/101

title: Improve reliability of restarts
description:
This change fixes a few issues that have been observed to put ZeroMQ into a bad state during a restart, leading to a freeze. Specifically, failing to call `disconnect()` on a client socket that has been disconnected on the server side, or attempting to send a message to a socket before the kernel is online.

The fix is somewhat heavy handed but should guard against most errors of this kind in the future. Specifically:

- The `JupyterSocket` class has been almost completely refactored and no longer exposes the underlying `zmq.Socket` -- it is now fully encapsulated so that we can guarantee consumers do not act on it in a way that could cause trouble. This ensures that e.g. we do not try to send messages to a disconnected socket, nor fail to disconnect the client end once the server side is disconnected.
- We no longer rely on the `connect_delay` event from ZeroMQ, since we cannot control its interval and in some states we don't receive it. Instead, we use our own timer to ensure that connection delays are logged every couple of seconds, and the connection fails entirely if it takes more than 10s. 
- We now reject restart (and shutdown) attempts if they occur while the kernel is not actually online. A major cause of restart freezes was allowing `shutdown` requests to proceed when the kernel was in the `Starting` state.

There are still some issues around restart, but they are less major. The biggest one (in my testing) is that if the kernel fails to start up after a restart attempt, you don't see that failure in the Console (it still says it's restarting). That happens because we don't emit startup failures on restarts, which is a separate issue, though probably still worth fixing.

Should address the following issues:
https://github.com/rstudio/positron/issues/667
https://github.com/rstudio/positron/issues/721

title: Handle empty elements and text-only elements in React HTML renderer
description:
This issue fixes a React error by handling some new cases in the HTML renderer: - Elements with a single `text` node now get rendered with text contents directly, instead of rendering the text inside its own ``. - Elements with no children, such as `
`, are now created without any children. It turns out that React throws a render exception if you create a `
` element with a child array, even if that child array is empty! This was the root cause of the reported issue. Addresses https://github.com/posit-dev/positron/issues/1195. Note, however, that because the HTML renderer is stripping scripts for safety, the rendered item we display isn't very helpful -- it looks expandable but can't be expanded. A better fix for this would be showing the element in a sandboxed frame so it could run scripts, but for Private Alpha, I think the best we can do is make it not blow up.

title: Use R_HOME to tell libR-sys where to find R
description: Addresses https://github.com/rstudio/positron/issues/580.

title: Add `extensionEnabledApiProposals` to Positron
description:
Addresses #911 

This PR adds the `extensionEnabledApiProposals` to Positron's `product.json`. After this change, the Jupyter extension works:

![Screenshot 2023-08-11 at 6 06 04 PM](https://github.com/rstudio/positron/assets/12505835/d66a12aa-93d5-4057-a53e-6a0c82f4d73e)


(Notice 👀 that variables defined in the notebook cells do not show up in the Environment pane.)

This PR [takes a page from vscodium's book](https://github.com/VSCodium/vscodium/pull/1187/files) and adds a shell script to automate this moving forward. I made this change by running the shell script manually, but eventually we'll want to do this on some cadence in an automated way. I'll open a follow-up issue to track that.

title: Improve Cmd+Enter behavior
description:
This change aligns Positron's Cmd+Enter behavior to be more like RStudio's in edge cases at the end of the file. In particular:

- If you Cmd+Enter on the last line of the file, a new line will be created at the end of the file. This is the most important part of the change; it lets you treat the editor surface more like a REPL.
- When you Cmd+Enter on a line of code and the rest of the file is empty, the cursor will be placed at the line after the code instead of at the end of the file.
- You no longer get an pop-up error if you Cmd+Enter and we can't find any code to run. Instead we "run" a blank line and don't advance the cursor.

Addresses https://github.com/rstudio/positron/issues/695, including adding RStudio's subtle behavior change when you Cmd+Enter on the last line of the file and that line is empty (we add a new line beneath the cursor when you do this, but don't navigate to it)

Addresses https://github.com/rstudio/positron/issues/876

title: Generate client instance IDs up front
description:
This change addresses an issue that results in error messages that look like this:

```
Client instance 'A5DA470D-337F-40C5-9552-D89770AC796C' not found; dropping message
```

Before the change, client instance (comm) IDs were returned by the extension host. Unfortunately, due to message ordering issues, this meant that we would sometimes get messages for the client delivered _before_ the client ID was returned, so those messages got dropped. This often included the initial payload for the environment pane.

After the change, we assign a client ID on the front end and immediately create a receiver before asking the back end to be created. This way, we're ready for messages right away. 

I've also changed the way we generate client IDs, so that they are more readable and it's more obvious what messages/logs pertain to. Instead of random UUIDs, they now look something like this for e.g. an Environment comm: `positron-environment-python-1-a5da470d`.

title: Add command to clear input history
description:
This change adds a command that clears the input history for the active language. When invoked, it thoroughly cleans history from:

- the stored/persisted copy of the history
- the in-memory input history cache in the execution history
- the REPL's history cache (so history navigation inside the editor doesn't pull up the deleted entries)

initial scaffolding for ark graphics device
description: This PR provides the initial scaffolding for the ark graphics device. The implementation is similar in spirit to the RStudio graphics device, but is vastly simpler: rather than define our own separate graphics device that forwards all relevant graphics events to a sub-device, we instead just monkey-patch an existing device with the hooks we need for graphics events. This PR also includes a "stub" so that generating a plot also causes that plot to be opened in Preview, just so you can be convinced something is happening. The next phase will be making sure that gets rendered somewhere in Positron instead :-)

Since this PR modifies `package.json` and `.vscode/tasks.json`, it's probably worth discussing if we should have some way of adding these without risking future merge conflicts...

title: Ensure all inputs are idle after an exit
description:
This change addresses a portion of https://github.com/rstudio/positron/issues/1038, in which a command that causes the runtime to crash can cause the last executed input to get stuck in a busy state. 

The fix is to ensure that when a runtime exits, all inputs are set to the idle state.

title: Defer reconnect to startup time
description:
This short change fixes https://github.com/posit-dev/positron/issues/1199, which is a regression from https://github.com/posit-dev/positron/pull/1008. 

In #1008, we deferred the creation of the Jupyter kernel wrapper until the runtime was actually asked to start. Because the reconnect code lives inside the kernel's constructor, some confusion results from calling it right before attempting to start the runtime.

The fix is to move the reconnect code from the kernel's constructor to its `start()` method, so that the constructor is mostly free of side effects, and `start()` is now smart enough to attach instead of starting if that's appropriate.

This is still not perfect, but it should do for private alpha (esp. given that end users are not prone to reloading the window in the desktop version; this is largely to fix things for our own dev team). A better solution will depend on https://github.com/posit-dev/positron/issues/1155 and https://github.com/posit-dev/positron/issues/1067.

title: Reconcile plot history navigation
description:
This change addresses https://github.com/rstudio/positron/issues/416 by making plot history navigation work the way more people expect. 

Specifically, the filmstrip now shows plots from oldest -> newest (top to bottom / left to right). 

While more people expect this behavior, it does mean that we need to fiddle with the scroll position as new plots are emitted, so that the newest (or at least most recently selected) plot is always visible in the filmstrip.

title: Use/build against R 3.5
Only await LSP stop when kernel is online
description:
Addresses an issue noted by @lionel- in https://github.com/rstudio/positron/issues/1038. 

In the cases of repeated, aggressive restarts, it is important to wait for the LSP to fully stop before attempting to start it again. It turns out that the only way to do this reliably is to wait for the `stop()` method to resolve (as it was before).

Therefore, we now need two codepaths -- one that we use it's safe to wait for `stop()` to return, and another that we use to shut down the LSP when the kernel has already exited. In both cases, we keep the new 2s timeout to keep the queue from getting blocked indefinitely.

title: use smarter markdown highlight rules
description: Closes https://github.com/rstudio/positron/issues/994.

title: Fix runtime state after an R crash.
description:
After an R crash and startup, the newly started instance of R doesn't work correctly (see #1038 for details).

This happens because when R crashes, the LSP client on the Positron side enters a broken state in which calling `stop()` returns a promise that never resolves. Since we use a `PQueue` for activation and deactivation, this unresolved promise blocks the queue forever and no further LSP activation or deactivation can be done.

The fix is as follows:
- Since `stop()`'s promise never resolves in this case, we listen for the `Stopped` state to arrive instead.
- A two-second timeout ensures that we never wait forever for the LSP to stop.
- Some cleanup to ensure event handlers are cleaned up after each activation and when the client is disposed.
 
Addresses https://github.com/rstudio/positron/issues/1038.

title: Don't wait for stdin after exiting
description:
This was once necessary to keep the kernel from shutting down prematurely, but is no longer necessary; it now appears to have an appropriate lifetime in `cargo test`, via `jupyter console`, and in Positron. 

Fixes https://github.com/rstudio/positron/issues/273.
