As macOS's heuristics for deciding when to prompt the user about network connections are opaque, I can't tell for sure if the issue is fixed or not, but I did run a full rebuild (which often results in getting prompted again) and didn't get prompted afterwards.

title: Ensure that comms closed when the associated runtime exits
description:
When a runtime exits, the comms associated with it don't necessarily get closed. This change ensures that they do by marking all connected comms as `closed` when the runtime exits. This prevents individual kernels from needing to do this accounting work during shutdown. 

Addresses https://github.com/rstudio/positron/issues/584.

title: Remove unused positron-plots-view-icon
description: It looks like issue https://github.com/rstudio/positron/issues/455 was caused by a typo; there exists both `positron-plots-view-icon` and `positron-plot-view-icon`. Only the latter is actually an icon, but the former is what the Plots pane refers to. This change removes the pluralized version, and switches the Plots pane to use the other version, which does actually have an icon.

title: Read initial state of plots pane from service
description: Reads the initial state of the Plots pane from the Plots headless service. This allows the pane to show plots that were emitted before the pane was open, and repopulates the pane correctly when it is moved/reattached to different locations in the UI.

title: Check for an existing environment instance before creating one
description:
Addresses https://github.com/posit-dev/positron/issues/1112. While poking at that issue, I realized it was more than a double-accounting error internally; we really do create extra environment instances as you restart runtimes. Restarting R, for example, leaves you with two Rs. 

![image](https://github.com/posit-dev/positron/assets/470418/a068b8eb-48ee-40eb-867d-527085fbef21)

The problem is that a restart generates both `onWillStartRuntime` events and `onDidReconnectRuntime` events, and we create environment instances in both of these codepaths. 

The fix is to create a function that can be used to ensure we have an environment instance active, and to call it from both places. This function has a new clause that tests to see whether there's already an instance alive for the runtime before it opens a new one.

title: Use std::os::raw::c_char for cross-platform compat
description:
Currently `harp::register` uses a raw type for character pointers, which is not cross platform compatible (a character is `i8` on some systems and `u8` on others) -- ran into this while attempting to compile on Linux.

The fix is to use `libc::c_char` which resolves to the correct character type for the operating system.

There are also a few trivial whitespace changes introduced by `rustfmt`.

title: stop trying to use R_Is_Running
description:
The most interesting part of this PR is here:

https://github.com/rstudio/positron/compare/bugfix/linux-compile?expand=1#diff-ff5706db2eed01587e3786b377b19b745bfc159ac589162862856c8bc45f50ddR35

Effectively, we now use a broadcast channel (a [bus](https://crates.io/crates/bus)) to broadcast that R has finished initialization to all consumers who may need to know.

This PR also moves from using `std` channels to `crossbeam` channels. See https://github.com/rstudio/positron/issues/173 for motivation.

Closes https://github.com/rstudio/positron/issues/171.
Closes https://github.com/rstudio/positron/issues/173.

title: Ignore session managers other than the first
description:
### Intent

This change addresses an issue reported by @blairj09 in which Positron can't start R or Python sessions. More context, and logs, in this Slack thread:

https://positpbc.slack.com/archives/C05M2EZCPGR/p1710369775412109

I was not able to reproduce the issue myself (nor have many other people on the same build), but the logs provided by James make it clear what's going on: somehow, a second, defunct instance of `MainThreadLanguageRuntime` is getting constructed and is trying to register itself as the session manager. 

After that happens, we use the defunct instance to attempt to start sessions, which it can't do since it isn't connected to any language packs.

### Approach

The fix is to only allow one `MainThreadLanguageRuntime` to be register itself; any subsequent attempts at registration are refused (with a logged warning).

The fix is really a band-aid; if we find that this issue merits more attention, we should spend some time figuring out how it's possible to have two instances of the proxy class.

### QA Notes

No repro for this one, unfortunately.

@blairj09 has tested a private release I built with the change (https://github.com/posit-dev/positron/actions/runs/8283858792) and confirmed it fixes the problem for him.

title: Add Positron notebooks initial work
description: ### Intent Add a very basic implementation of a new notebook interface. ### Approach The notebooks are currently structured like the other React-based editors/widgets added to Positron (the data explorer and console.) There is an instance class (`PositronNotebookInstance`) that acts as the main dispatch for working with notebooks. This instance, once attached to an editor/input renders the notebook using React. Right now the notebooks are the very bare minimum of functional. You can write and run code cells but that's about it. E.g. no markdown cells, no rich html output. Basically, the notebooks are not meant to be used by anyone in their current state. There is a feature flag for enabling the notebooks that is under the `positron.notebooks.usePositronNotebooks` config key.

description:
### Intent

title: Feature/data explorer filtering & modal React rendering updates
description: ### Intent This PR is the result of starting work on the Data Explorer filtering feature. As this work progressed, it was time to do a lot of rework on how modal React rendering works (for React-based dialogs, context menus, and custom popups). #### PositronModalReactRenderer The `PositronModalDialogReactRenderer` and `PositronModalPopupReactRenderer` classes have been merged into a new `PositronModalReactRenderer` class that works for every kind of modal React component in Positron. Additionally, the `PositronModalReactRenderer` has been enhanced to support modal React components within other modal React components. #### Automatic layout The `DataExplorer` and `DataGrid` components now have "automatic layout" using `ResizeObserver`s. This means that we do not have to use prop drilling to get the size of these components into them. Over time, I will be reworking other React components like Console, Help, Variables, and Plots to support automatic layout. #### Improved Accessibility A number of improvements were made to the `PositronModalDialog` and `PositronModalPopup` components to support better keyboard navigation. `PositronModalPopup`s now support two styles of `KeyboardNavigation`: `dialog` and `menu`. In `dialog`-style keyboard navigation, the user presses Tab or Shift-Tab to navigate through focusable elements. In `list`-style keyboard navigation, the user presses Down Arrow or Up Arrow to navigate through focusable elements. #### PositronModalDialogs service We now have a "Show Example Modal Dialog" action that shows an example modal dialog. This action is only available when IsDevelopmentContext is true. As a resource for developers, this example modal dialog will be updated to have examples of every type of component that can appear in a modal dialog. At the moment, it looks like this: ![image](https://github.com/posit-dev/positron/assets/853239/27028c57-5cc9-4fd7-b2f5-8c7d7ae22bf7) #### Button and PositronButton components I am in the process of migrating every button we have in React components to be based on a new `Button` component that lives in `src/vs/base/browser/ui/positronComponents/button`. Prior to this work, we had a mishmash of raw `` tags and `` components in our UI. This rework is ongoing. When it is complete, the `PositronButton` component will be removed. #### ComboBox component I am in the process of building a new `ComboBox` component. This component will offer two modes of operation: drop-down list box and combo box. In this PR, only the drop-down list box is working. Here's how it looks: #### ContextMenu component A number of improvements were made to the new `ContextMenu` component. It now has better theming support, adjusted border radiuses, uses the new `Button` component and has a `left` or `right` alignment option. #### HorizontalSplitter & VerticalSplitter components Updated `z-index`. #### FilterBar component Lots of work was done on the filter bar component to updated it to the latest design (where it's just used for so-called "row filtering"). #### AddRowFilter modal popup Work has started on the AddRowFilter modal popup. ### QA Notes Since this PR includes a lot of reworking to how modal react components are rendered, we should be on the lookout for new regressions.

title: Add multi-session support to Positron
description: This change adds the infrastructure necessary to support multiple sessions per interpreter to Positron. Its primary payload is support for making notebook sessions first-class citizens in Positron that can be connected to any of Positron's UI components, but it also addresses a number of other issues and is designed to support other multi-session scenarios. Primarily addresses https://github.com/posit-dev/positron/issues/1625. Also addresses (directly or indirectly): https://github.com/posit-dev/positron/issues/1123 https://github.com/posit-dev/positron/issues/2022 https://github.com/posit-dev/positron/issues/1067 https://github.com/posit-dev/positron/issues/634 https://github.com/posit-dev/positron/issues/1456 Depends on (needs merge coordinated with) https://github.com/posit-dev/positron-python/pull/413. ## Approach Before this change, Positron had a single interface for language runtimes, which bundled two concepts into a class called `LanguageRuntime`: - a language runtime's `metadata` (its path, icon, ID, etc.) - controls for interacting with the runtime, such as starting it, stopping it, listening for messages, etc. The main change in this PR is the unbundling of these two concepts into separate entities: `LanguageRuntimeMetadata` for the first and `LanguageRuntimeSession` for the second. Language packs no longer need to provide both of these objects at once; now, it is only necessary to provide the metadata to tell Positron what runtimes are available. When Positron is ready to start a session, it uses the metadata to ask the language pack to start a new session. The session object that is returned contains the controls for interacting with that specific session. ## Services Before this change, a single `LanguageRuntimeService` handled everything associated with runtimes. I have decomposed this service into three separate services in order to keep the original service from becoming too monolithic. Because services cannot have cyclic dependencies, the dependency graph is unidirectional: ```mermaid graph TD session[RuntimeSessionService] -- get registrations --> runtime[LangaugeRuntimeService] startup[RuntimeStartupService] -- get registrations --> runtime startup -- autostart sessions --> session ``` ### LanguageRuntimeService This service is a shell of its former self. All it does is provide a store of runtimes that are currently registered, and notify interested parties when that set changes. It could also be called the `RuntimeRegistrationService`. ### RuntimeSessionService This service provides facilities for maintaining the set of active runtime sessions of all kinds, including "console" sessions (the only kind understood prior to this PR) and "notebook" sessions (the kind introduced here). Requests to start new sessions, query the set of active sessions, etc. all go through the `RuntimeSessionService`. ### RuntimeStartupService This service manages the tangled and asynchronous process that coordinates the startup of, and/or reconnection to, the correct runtime(s) for the current workspace. It attempts to organize this process into a sequence of well-defined phases. ## Extension Model The language packs have undergone significant changes to support this work. Most notably, the concept of a "provider" that creates a runtime from metadata is gone. In its place is a new concept: a `RuntimeManager`. It has three responsibilities: 1. **Discovery**. The manager provides a way to discover the available runtimes on the machine 2. **Create a new session**. The manager provides a way to create a new session for a given runtime. 3. **Reconnect to an existing session**. The manager provides a way to rejoin an existing session, given the runtime _and_ identifying information about the session to connect to. These changes have enabled a number of improvements to the language packs. Moving a lot of code that use to run at startup time to session creation time has improved performance and fixed a number of bugs. ## Session Startup Sequence The session startup process typically works as follows: 1. A request is received to start a new session from a given runtime. 2. A unique ID is generated for the new session. 3. Positron looks up the extension-supplied runtime manager that is associated with the runtime ID. 4. Positron asks the extension's runtime manager to provision a new session. 5. The language pack gets the new session ready to start (but does not start it!). It forms the Jupyter kernel arguments, creates methods, etc. 6. The language pack returns a session object to Positron. 7. Positron informs all interested parties that a new session has been created and is about to start. Anyone who's interested in the session can attach listeners before it begins starting up. 8. Positron asks the new session to start. 9. The startup sequence proceeds as it does today. The most notable difference from how things work today is the provisioning step; it takes the place of the creation of the `LanguageRuntime` object, which used to occur at discovery time. ## Debugging tools Finally, this change also includes a debugging tool that lets you: - see a list of all active sessions, their mode, and their status - see detailed information about the runtime associated with each session - manually start/restart/etc. the session, or jump to its output log - see a list of active comms for the session along with a message counter for each (to watch traffic) - disconnect any comm The tool is only intended for developers and fairly advanced debugging, so it's hidden by default. To turn it on, go here:

title: Fortify R installation discovery on Windows
description:
Addresses #2393 

This PR raises our bar for discovering and prioritizing R installations on Windows, hopefully accounting for more scenarios we are going to see in the wild.

Highlights:

* Consults the registry when determining the current/default R version. This is the most official way of recording the current R version.
* `winreg` is a new dependency, so that we can read from the registry. This means everyone needs to `yarn` after we merge this PR.
* Lots of logic moved from being inline to going into helpers, to finesse the added complexity of having nontrivial "windows vs not-windows" branches.
* Explicit prioritization of `R_HOME/bin/x64/R.exe` as the binpath over `R_HOME/bin/R.exe`.
* If we don't learn the current version from the registry, but we find R on the `PATH` because of how rig works on Windows, we read that `.bat` file to learn the R version.

title: Updates/console improvements
description: This PR does several things: 1 - It brings `ansi-output` back into Positron as source code instead of of an NPM package. I did this for a couple reasons. The main one is that (I / we) need to be able to work on the `ANSIOutput` class more efficiently than having it in an NPM package allows. Additionally, importing `ansi-output` from an NPM package was causing this import problem: Which was not readily resolvable. Also, what was I thinking? I shouldn't have put it in an NPM package so soon. 2 - It moves duplicated functionality from `ActivityItemOutputStream` and `ActivityItemErrorStream` into a new base class called `ActivityItemStream`. Now, `ActivityItemOutputStream` and `ActivityItemErrorStream` just extend `ActivityItemStream` with no additional functionality. (This work was important for # 3.) 3 - It updates the `RuntimeItemActivity` class and the `ActivityItemStream` class so that `stdout` and `stderr` streams are optimally broken into lines of output. Prior to this work, if you were to execute the following R code fragment: ```R for (x in 1:5000) { Sys.sleep(0.02) print(sprintf("Lorem ipsum dolor sit amet, consectetur adipiscing elit %d.", x)) } ``` All 5,000 lines of output would wind up in a single, merged `ActivityItemOutputStream`. After this work, that code fragment will result in 5,000 `ActivityItemOutputStream` items, one per line of output. This work sets the stage for another PR coming soon that will trim Console output to some number of lines (1,000, 10,000, whatever that winds up being, TBD.) 4 - It brings back the scroll lock feature in Console. It also adds support for Home, End, Page Up, Page Down keys.

To address this, `PositronProxy` now inserts a set of default styles just after the `` tag in every proxied help document. With these default styles, this R help document now appears as: in the Positron Dark theme and: in the Positron Light theme. Notes: This is a bit of an arms race. There may be other help scenarios in R or Python that produce un-styled or badly-styled help output, and we may need to add additional default styles to the set of default styles that are added by `PositronProxy` or add updates the R.css file in Amalthea. Please open new issues for these problems! Also, I have moved the "help is unstyled on first open" problem to its own issue: https://github.com/posit-dev/positron/issues/1657

title: 1644 help focus lost when help is shown
description:
This PR addresses #1644.

In the initial implementation of the `WebviewFindDelegate` in `HelpEntry`, we were shifting focus into the help overlay webview when the `focus` method of the delegate was called. This was causing focus to get ripped away from whatever view caused the help topic to be displayed. It turns out that this was unnecessary because this method is only called when the `WebviewFindWidget` is hidden and we don't need to / want to shift focus anywhere in this case. This was the best fix.

title: 981 add minimize button to console
description: This PR updates the panel part to have minimize, maximize, and restore buttons when it is positioned on the bottom and aligned center (which is the default positioning and alignment). It was very difficult to sort out how we could "add minimize button to console" and support all the positioning and alignment scenarios. After a lot of experimentation, I found that it felt best to add explicit actions for minimize, maximize, and restore, and to enable those actions only when the panel was positioned on the bottom and aligned center. Instead of conditionalizing these actions and having their icons appear and disappear, I felt it was better to leave the icons always visible and discoverable in the panel: Here's a movie of these action in motion: https://github.com/posit-dev/positron/assets/853239/d35d1009-e97f-447b-ac67-c22d592630aa When the panel is positioned left or right, it retains the standard Visual Studio Code "toggle maximized panel" behavior. Left: Left maximized: Right: Right maximized: When the panel is not aligned center, the new minimize, maximize, and restore actions are unavailable, as is "toggle maximized panel". This is a limitation of Workbench, as documented in `the workbench grid currently prevents us from supporting panel maximization with non-center panel alignment` comment in `panelActions.ts`.

title: #233 console should support hyperlinks in output
description: This PR updates ANSIOutput - adding support for parsing Operating System Command escape sequences and OSC 8 (Anchor). You can read more about OSC 8 here: https://iterm2.com/3.2/documentation-escape-codes.html In R, you can test this by executing these commands: ```R library(cli) cat("This is a", style_hyperlink("Google", "https://google.com"), "link.\n") style_hyperlink("Google", "https://google.com") cli::cli_text("Google! {.url https://google.com}.") cat("\x1b]8;;http://www.google.com\x1b\x5cThis is a Google Link\x1b]8;;\x1b\x5c") ``` When you do, you'll see: Each of the Google links can be opened using ⌘+Click on macOS. (Ctrl+Click on Windows). Much work remains! We still have to sort out all the different OSC 8 scenarios we'll support.

title: Updates/improve console url handling
description:
This PR updates file-scheme URL handling. 

You can test this out using:

```R
library(cli)

# Files
cli_text("Click {.file ~/.zshrc} to edit your .zshrc file.")
cli_text("Click {.file ~/.zshrc:7:8} to edit line 7 column 5 of your .zshrc file.")
cli_text("Click {.file ~/.zshrc:10:5} to edit line 10 column 5 of your .zshrc file.")
```

And:

```R
library(cli)

# Files
cli_text("Please visit {.href [.zshrc](file:///Users/brian/.zshrc)} to Brian's .zshrc file.")
cli_text("Please visit {.href [.zshrc](file:///Users/brian/.zshrc#17,5)} to Brian's .zshrc file.")
```

After picking suitable URLs that will open on your machine.

Note: I plan to add an href URL conversion feature in another PR that will map file URLs in this format:

```R
file:///Users/brian/.zshrc:17:5
```

into this format:

```R
file:///Users/brian/.zshrc#17,5
```

Because I believe users will generate URLs like this.

title: Support file URLS in file:line:col and file:line format
description:
This PR updates OSC 8 file URL handling so that URLs in the form:

```
file:///Users/brian/.zshrc:17:5
file:///Users/brian/.zshrc:5
```

Are supported and properly navigate to the `:line:col` or `:line` specified.

To test this, execute the following R code replacing the file URL with something that's valid on your machine.

```R
cli_text("Please visit {.href [.zshrc](file:///Users/brian/.zshrc:17:5)} to Brian's .zshrc file.")
cli_text("Please visit {.href [.zshrc](file:///Users/brian/.zshrc:5)} to Brian's .zshrc file.")
```

Here's a long list of file URLs that should work:

```R
# Files
cli_text("Click {.file ~/.zshrc} to edit your .zshrc file.")
cli_text("Click {.file ~/.zshrc:7:5} to edit line 7 column 5 of your .zshrc file.")
cli_text("Click {.file ~/.zshrc:10:5} to edit line 10 column 5 of your .zshrc file.")
cli_text("Please visit {.href [.zshrc](file:///Users/brian/.zshrc)} to Brian's .zshrc file.")

```

title: Addresses 1806 by adjusting how the Positron Console is activated and focused
description:
This PR addresses #1806.

- It adjusts how Workbench `Layout`'s `restorePanel` method works so that the Panel isn't unnecessarily restored when it isn't minimized or maximized. There is an updated comment in this code which more fully documents when the Panel should be restored.

- It relayers the `PositronConsoleService` from the `common` layer to the `browser` layer so that it can access `browser` services (in particular, the `IWorkbenchLayoutService`).

- **Whenever** code is executed in the `PositronConsoleService`, the Panel is restored, if necessary, and the Console view is opened. There are currently no scenarios where code should be _silently_ executed through the `PositronConsoleService` (i.e. without showing the Console view).

- Focus is driven into the Positron Console when appropriate.

- When code is executed using ⌘-Enter (macOS) or Ctrl-Enter (Windows/Linux), focus is NOT driven into the Positron Console.

A little movie:

https://github.com/posit-dev/positron/assets/853239/7cafda4b-6acc-4e3b-bae5-ba34e956d1b2

title: Enable cli.hyperlink_run and add support for opening x-r-run resources
description: This PR adds the final piece of the puzzle to be able to address https://github.com/posit-dev/positron/issues/1469 (see design doc https://github.com/posit-dev/positron/issues/1769). With this PR, the following R hyperlinks are supported: ```R # Email cli::cli_text("Please email {.email brian.lambert@posit.co} for more information.") cli::cli_text("Please email {.href [Brian Lambert](mailto:brian.lambert@posit.co)} for more information.") # File cli::cli_text("Click {.file ~/.zshrc} to edit your .zshrc file.") cli::cli_text("Click {.file ~/.zshrc:7:5} to edit line 17 column 5 of your .zshrc file.") cli::cli_text("Click {.file ~/.zshrc:10:5} to edit line 10 column 5 of your .zshrc file.") cli::cli_text("Please visit {.href [.zshrc](file:///Users/brian/.zshrc)} to open Brian's .zshrc file.") cli::cli_text("Please visit {.href [.zshrc](file:///Users/brian/.zshrc#17,5)} to open Brian's .zshrc file.") cli::cli_text("Please visit {.href [.zshrc](file:///Users/brian/.zshrc#5)} to open Brian's .zshrc file.") # URL cli::cli_text("Please visit {.url https://posit.co} to learn about us.") cli::cli_text("Please visit {.href [Posit PBC](https://posit.co)} to learn about us.") # Help - function cli::cli_text("Help on function {.help rlang::abort}") # Help - topic cli::cli_text("Help on function {.topic rlang::args_dots_empty}") # Vignette. cli::cli_text("Help on vignette {.vignette dplyr::grouping}") # Runnable code cli::cli_text("Help on run {.run rlang::abort('oh no')}") ``` Note that at the moment, help, vignette, and run hyperlinks do not actually open, but do write to the console indicating that they were clicked. There is a separate issue https://github.com/posit-dev/positron/issues/1906 tracking this work.

title: Mark Rust files as `@generated` for rustfmt
description:
Results in https://github.com/posit-dev/amalthea/pull/241

Minor tweak to the comm generator that generates the Rust files with `// @generated` at the top.

This allows a project wide call to `rustfmt` (i.e. `cargo +nightly fmt -v`) to ignore these files. Eventually they have plans to make it so that format-on-save while inside those files will also pick up on `@generated` and not reformat it, but that doesn't currently work (but that's ok, we don't typically touch these rust files unless we are debugging something).
https://github.com/rust-lang/rustfmt/blob/8486837d557c152fee52383852835d4941602423/src/formatting.rs#L79-L80

The alternative is to try and run fmt on the files during generation time to ensure that they comply with our rules, but that would require everyone to have an up to date nightly version of rust installed and I just didn't feel like it was worth the pain of trying to set up and enforce that. (I saw we do it for python with black, but even that caused me a little pain to get it set up)

Now that we're able to vendor Python dependencies without affecting the user's environment, I'd like to vote for going back to Pydantic.

title: Use more portable paths in the test explorer
description:
Addresses https://github.com/posit-dev/positron/issues/1808#issuecomment-1920164409

With the R extension's log level set to "debug", you can get this info about the error:

```
Error: ℹ Loading vscodereporter
Error: '\U' used without hex digits in character string (<input>:1:32)
Execution halted
```

I was able to reproduce the problem in a windows VM and this fixes it for me.

Relevant context:

* Prior to this PR, the test-running command looked something like this:

    ```
    "C:\Program Files\R\R-4.3.2\bin\R.exe" --no-echo -e "devtools::load_all('d:/Users/jenny/source/repos/positron/extensions/positron-r/resources/testing/vscodereporter');devtools::test_active_file('d:\Users\jenny\source\repos\rematch2\tests\testthat\test-all.R', desc = 'corner cases', reporter = VSCodeReporter)"
    ```

    Note the paths in the snippet of R code and, specifically, the different path separators. The problem was the Windows-style path where the backslashes aren't escaped, i.e. doubled. In the error above, you can tell that the `load_all()` command actually succeeds, so it's the path in `test_active_file()` that is the problem. The solution is to use POSIX-style path separation. Here's how the test-running command looks with this PR:

    ```
    "C:\Program Files\R\R-4.3.2\bin\R.exe" --no-echo -e "devtools::load_all('d:/Users/jenny/source/repos/positron/extensions/positron-r/resources/testing/vscodereporter');devtools::test_active_file('d:/Users/jenny/source/repos/rematch2/tests/testthat/test-exec.R',reporter = VSCodeReporter)"
    ```
* This treatment was already in place for the path to the embedded test reporter package and now it's clear why. https://github.com/posit-dev/positron/blob/9362409efbe4b15b75c4ab713ee3ae57cf60f464/extensions/positron-r/src/testing/runner-testthat.ts#L17-L19
* This approach is consistent with the advice given in the [R for Windows FAQ](https://cran.r-project.org/bin/windows/base/rw-FAQ.html#R-can_0027t-find-my-file):

  > Backslashes have to be doubled in R character strings, so for example one needs `"d:\\R-4.3.2\\library\\xgobi\\scripts\\xgobi.bat"`. You can make life easier for yourself by using forward slashes as path separators: they do work under Windows. 
* FWIW `child_process.spawn(..., { shell: true })` is launching a `cmd.exe` shell on Windows, but this turns out to be neither here nor there in terms of this problem.

title: Forward fully adjusted console input width on to API consumers
description: Addresses https://github.com/posit-dev/positron/issues/2074 Addresses https://github.com/posit-dev/positron/issues/2176 I'm like 75% confident this is the right fix, so someone who knows more should definitely judge this PR. In the first commit, you'll see two variables: - `adjustedWidth`: The width of the console after taking the padding into account - `consoleInputWidth`: The width of the console after also taking the vertical scrollbar into account If this video is anything to go by, I believe that the downstream consumers of `getConsoleWidth()` really need `consoleInputWidth`, not `adjustedWidth`. i.e. it looks like the vertical scrollbar is embedded into the console instance in a way that it definitely affects how many characters can be printed in the console by R/Python. I suppose _technically_ we may want to go through and update the functions from `getConsoleWidth()` -> `getConsoleInputWidth()` and whatnot, but honestly this is probably the only variant of "console width" that extensions will probably care about, so I'm satisfied with just tweaking the docs a little (i can revert that too if you don't even want to go that far) https://github.com/posit-dev/positron/assets/19150088/8edf0290-0f55-4c3c-a2a5-6b8a8cd15502

title: Remove `libR-sys` specific tweaks
description:
- [x] Bump ark version

Requires https://github.com/posit-dev/amalthea/pull/205

With https://github.com/posit-dev/amalthea/pull/205, we no longer depend on libR-sys. More importantly, we now link to the R API _dynamically_ and _fully at runtime_. This has many many benefits, as outlined in https://github.com/posit-dev/amalthea/pull/205, but the most important ones here are:

- We don't need the `DYLD_FALLBACK_LIBRARY_PATH` hacks anymore. This was only required on macOS, and was the way that `ark` found the correct `libR.dylib` on startup. We no longer need to find `libR.dylib` immediately _at startup_. Instead, we locate `libR.dylib` (or `R.dll` or `libR.so`) relative to `R_HOME` from within ark itself and open the shared library at runtime from within ark, and then set up all the R API bindings from there.
- For essentially the same reasons, we don't need to add the folder that contains `R.dll` to the `PATH` on Windows (that was how Windows did dependency lookup at start up time).

The 2nd bullet is particularly nice, because we already got a report where one of our QA engineers had another R related path on the `PATH` that pointed to a different R version's `R.dll` than the one they were trying to start up, which caused a crash. We aren't entirely sure how he had that in the PATH, but it's nice that this avoids that possibility altogether.

description: I think it would be nice to be able to target one (or more) comms for code generation, so that you can just work on "your thing", even if there's some unsynched work in other comms. I'm also reducing/changing the amount of output.

title: Use same `clear-all` icon in Console as search, output, debug etc
description:
Addresses #1559

This was bothering me again today and has come up in usability testing. We have feedback that our `'positron-clear-pane'` icon looks like it will _close_ the console, rather than clear it. As @gtritchie points out, this `'clear-all'` icon is the one that means "clear this thing" for Search, Output, the Debug Console, etc.

title: Support for hierarchies of objects in connections.
description:
Targets #2042 
Also see https://github.com/posit-dev/amalthea/pull/204
This adds support for hierarchies within database connections. 

We introduce a new `ConnectionItemNode` type that's used for intermediate objects that are not the database root and the leaf like tables.  Connection nodes track their own path in the tree so we can easily retrieve their children if we want to.
We also added a POC usage in Zed to make it easier for testing.

Now the `tables_request` RPC method has a larger scope other than simply returning tables, so we might want to rename it to `list_objects` to match the connections contract, but I think this could go in a different PR.

The easiest way to test is to use Zed:

```
connection hello
```

https://github.com/posit-dev/positron/assets/4706822/b0d4c82b-3c4f-4337-a657-f51780dce12f

title: Set `ARK_R_VERSION` and `ARK_R_DYNAMIC_LIBRARY_PATH`
description:
Joint PR with https://github.com/posit-dev/amalthea/pull/180

- R version because it makes it so much easier on ark if positron-r just passes it through this way
- Dynamic lib path so ark utilities can perform dynamic symbol resolution at runtime

title: Minor revisions to data tool openrpc contract to track positron-python work
description:
* Refer to columns by index rather than name (to avoid ambiguity)
* Use `=` instead of `==` for equality comparison enum (it generates `Eq` instead of `EqEq` in the generated enum)

Related: https://github.com/posit-dev/positron-python/pull/316

title: Ensure each R runtime is registered only once
description:
Addresses https://github.com/posit-dev/positron/issues/2072 and several related issues.

The underlying issue here is that the R extension can register the same R version multiple times (e.g. once when asked to provide a specific version of R, and a second time when asked to discover all R versions). This can create a situation where the runtime ID is not unique, and consequently we try to run methods (like `check_installed`) on the wrong one.

The fix is as follows:
- Most importantly, don't create multiple runtimes with the same ID. If Positron asks for a runtime we've already provided, use the exact instance that was previously returned.
- Refactor the `RRuntimeManager` a little so that its private map isn't exposed and we can guarantee safe access. 
- Use a more idiomatic TypeScript singleton pattern for the `RRuntimeManager`, so it's very obvious at the call sites that a global singleton is being engaged.

(More could be done here but wanted to keep this small since it's affecting several scenarios)

title: Rationalize interactions with the R runtime(s)
description:
This PR is motivated by me trying to use the new `checkInstalled()` facilities in the testing feature, as promised in https://github.com/posit-dev/positron/issues/1629#issuecomment-1852712896.

As it stands the "check installed" feature requires an explicit handle for the running R runtime (i.e. you call `runtime.checkInstalled(...)`), which in turn requires having a `Map` of all the R runtimes registered with the extension host (i.e. first you must call `runtime = getRunningRRuntime(runtimes)`, where `runtimes` is currently provisioned in positron-r's `activate()` function, then passed around.

This PR started as an attempt to make it so that fewer functions and features need to know about this `runtimes` map, then grew to also include the `lastRuntimePath`.

This has become my main question:

What's the intent of the `runtimePath` in `LanguageRuntimeMetadata`? At least in the R extension, what we seem to need downstream is not `runtimePath`, but instead what I've introduced here as `runtimeBinpath` = the path to an R executable. When the metadata only includes `runtimePath`, we end up re-creating the binpath in various places, in different ways in the extension, which I think we should avoid. I'll make some more comments inline.

title: Remove stray dollar sign
description: Sadly I'm seeing this pop-up alot right now, so I happened to notice this.

title: Add handling for escape key in activity prompt
description:
Addresses #1148 

This is now more consistent with canceling out of Positron console input, as well as more consistent with RStudio behavior.

I do _not_ believe we need to do anything else about checking for more modifiers in the activity prompt; it already does the right thing for <kbd>ctrl</kbd>+<kbd>shift</kbd>+<kbd>c</kbd> and similar, i.e. it does not treat that as if it were <kbd>ctrl</kbd>+<kbd>c</kbd>.

title: New `startAffiliatedLanguageRuntimes()` method
description:
Addresses #1067 with another small-ish, iterative change

This PR adds a new method for the `LanguageRuntimeService` that starts up any affiliated language runtimes, instead of trying to do this in the constructor. Organized like this, we can call this _from_ the `MainThreadLanguageRuntime` constructor like `this._languageRuntimeService.startAffiliatedLanguageRuntimes()` at the right time, i.e. ***after*** the `onDidRequestLanguageRuntime` listener gets created.

This PR does not actually move it over there yet, because we need to be able to start up an extension with a runtime provider request (which we don't do yet).

title: Python: add None default for optional dataclass fields when generating comm stubs
description:
This greatly improves the ergonomics of data classes that have optional fields (see, e.g. objects with few required fields in data_tool-backend-openrpc.json). For example, to be able to write:

```python
c = ColumnSchema(name='a', type_name='string')
```

as opposed to having to write out a bunch of None parameters for the optional ColumnSchema fields. 

The only downside of this is that there is some validation benefit to requiring a JSON key to be present (e.g. `"description": null`). This seems like an acceptable trade-off, though.

title: OpenRPC: Also emit non-object component type aliases for Python in code generator
description: This just replicates the type aliases as with Rust and TypeScript (there is an instance of this being done in the DataTool comm)

title: Add `positron.runtime.restartOnCrash` option
description:
When an unexpected crash occurs, Positron now automatically restarts the runtime. When this occurs during development this makes it hard to find relevant information in the logs because of all the log noise from the restart. To avoid this, I propose adding a `restartOnCrash` configuration option.

This PR adds such an option scoped under `positron>runtime`. When restart is disabled we show a restart button in the console instead of automatically restarting.

title: force execution of code cells, even for invalid/incomplete code
description:
This is achieved by adding a `force` argument to `positron.runtime.executeCode`. If true, we do not check with the runtime's `isCodeFragmentComplete` and instead immediately execute code.

Addresses #2009. See https://github.com/posit-dev/positron/issues/2009#issuecomment-1883317048 for my motivation for solving the issue by directly executing the code.

I'm not sure about the name `force`. It isn't very clear but I couldn't think of a better alternative. Maybe `skipIsCodeFragmentComplete` / `skipIsComplete` / `skipChecks` / something else?

title: Implement `Console` API with `pasteText()` POC
description:
Addresses https://github.com/posit-dev/positron/issues/1507
Addresses https://github.com/posit-dev/positron/issues/2024

> Note: I first renamed `mainThreadConsole.ts` -> `mainThreadConsoleService.ts` (and the corresponding objects, and the corresponding `extHost*.ts` files) because it was really about the positron console _service_ (i.e. the onDidChangeWidth event lives in the service). Later on I had to recreate `mainThreadConsole.ts`, but this time it was really about a single console instance. Unfortunately this makes the diffs of that file a little annoying to look at.

This PR introduces a new `Console` API, which has 1 function for now, `pasteText()`. You can get a `Console` by calling the other new function, `positron.window.getConsoleForLanguage('r')`.

It works by mimicking what is done in the `TextEditor` API. i.e. there is a simple string `id` that is the key that ties an `ExtHostConsole` to the backend `MainThreadConsole`. In our case, for now, that `id` is the language id. When a `Console` instance is created, that `id` gets embedded in its functions, so the API functions don't need it as an argument.

https://github.com/posit-dev/positron/assets/19150088/e8f1bcb1-0e82-4214-9d9d-5b4dab6555c5

title: Support for frontend-side RPC methods
description:
Progress towards #1542

- Add a `methods` namespace to `positron.d.ts`. This namespace contains the main entry point for calling a method, `methods.call()`, as well as all individual methods, only `lastActiveTextEditorContext()` at the moment.

  I chose to start with a partial implementation of `lastActiveTextEditorContext()` that returns the URI for the currently active editor because it is sufficient to support important usethis methods like `usethis::use_test()` and `usethis::use_r()` (these switch between test and source files).

  `methods.call()` is designed to directly interface with RPC mechanisms. It takes a method name and an object of parameters and takes care of matching the relevant method, checking the parameters according to the OpenRPC contract, calling the method, and returning an appropriate JSON-RPC response object (either a result or an error). It never throws and instead returns JSON-RPC error responses.

  I created a namespace containing all individual methods to make it easy to call the methods from the typescript side of the runtime extensions.

- Add `last_active_editor_context` and `debug_sleep` frontend methods in `frontend-frontend-openrpc.json`. The latter method is useful to generate a long-running method call for testing purposes, e.g. to trigger a user interrupt while a method is running. The `debug` methods are not exposed in the `methods` namespace.

- Add support for frontend-side requests in `generate-comms.ts`.

- In the Jupyter runtime adapter, add support for receiving RPC requests from the frontend comm via the StdIn socket. It's not possible to use a normal `comm_msg` message for these requests because the reply would be queued on the `Shell` socket which doesn't support concurrent processing of messages (see https://github.com/jupyter/jupyter_client/issues/433), causing a deadlock. So instead we send requests via `StdIn` using the same model as `input_request`.

  The backend waits for a reply on the StdIn socket synchronously. This means that only one comm (e.g. the frontend comm) can send a request at a time but this could be extended to support concurrent requests from other comms if needed.

title: Implement `x-r-run` handler
description:
- [x] Bump amalthea requirement

Requires https://github.com/posit-dev/amalthea/pull/194
Addresses https://github.com/posit-dev/positron/issues/1906 (Mostly)

Need https://github.com/posit-dev/positron/issues/1507 so we can get the active Console to be able to put manually runnable `code` onto the user's Console input prompt. Right now I am just writing it to the clipboard as a temporary workaround.

There are 3 categories of `code` that can come through `x-r-run`:

- **Not Runnable**: Code that isn't safe to run, or doesn't look like R code. We use a regular expression to check if the R code is in the "safe" format we expect, following these guidelines https://cli.r-lib.org/reference/links.html#security-considerations. Modeled after RStudio's https://github.com/rstudio/rstudio/blob/a8afd4453b535ec80e49b410c302f6881279888b/src/gwt/src/org/rstudio/core/client/hyperlink/RunHyperlink.java#L98.

- **Manually Runnable**: Looks safe enough for the user to run, but isn't from a "blessed" R package and the package in question isn't attached. Ideally if the user clicks this we then put the code on their Console input prompt, but right now we can't do that so instead it copies to clipboard.

- **Automatically Runnable**: Safe enough to run automatically. Either comes from a blessed package like rlang, or the user has attached the package in question and it passed our regex check. This uses `RRuntime`'s `execute()` method to fire off the code. Note that there is a bug in the Console that prevents code being fired in this manner from showing up in the Console history immediately.


https://github.com/posit-dev/positron/assets/19150088/8dcf89d8-3ccc-4591-bdb5-fd3984cf913e

title: pass enter key events on multiline statements to the code editor widget
description:
This is one approach to addressing https://github.com/posit-dev/positron/issues/1552.

The idea is to only consume the Enter key event if we actually execute code. If the runtime says that the code fragment is incomplete, or if the user hits Shift+Enter, we don't consume the key event and let the code editor widget handle it. The code editor widget already auto-indents based on the configuration for the language.

One downside in Python is that if you have a multiline statement like:

```python
if 1:
    print("Hello<cursor>")
```

where `<cursor>` represents your cursor position (which is common since the closing `")` is added automatically), and you press enter, you will end up pushing the `")` to the next line instead of executing since the statement is not complete. This is consistent with IPython but not a great UX IMO. I think that is something to be handled in the Python runtime's `isCodeFragmentComplete` though.

@softwarenerd I'm curious to hear what your thoughts are on this approach.

title: Use new OpenRPC mechanism to implement frontend comm
description:
Follow-up to #1942.
Progress towards #265.
Also progress towards #1542 as we need to integrate the reverse frontend RPCs in the new comm infrastructure.

This ports the frontend comm to use the new infrastructure for generated comms and message types.

The frontend events were straightforward to port. They just required adding generation of event enums to the TS files. This enum is used to merge the various frontend event into a single message type tagged with the runtime ID, and then fan them back out at the handling sites.

The implementation of backend RPCs side-steps some more difficult questions about the role of `callMethod()` and its place in the positron API (issue upcoming).

- Currently the comms are main-thread entities but the main users of `callMethod()` are extensions. There is no straightforward way of reusing the `performRpc()` implementation of `PositronBaseComm` from the extensions. So I've left a duplicated implementation inside positron-r.

- It's not obvious whether the `callMethod()` API should be generic across runtimes, specific to runtimes, or a mix. I've left it unspecified for now. This is supported in `generate-comms.ts` by treating empty object specs with `additionalProperties: true` as a kind of "any" dictionary/struct. In Python this maps to `JsonData` and in Rust this maps to `serde_json::Value`. The parameter and result types are (un)specified this way.

With these changes I was able to remove the old event generation mechanism.

Before merging this we need to first merge the companion PRs for positron-python and amalthea.

title: For workspace affiliation, store runtime metadata instead of only runtime ID
description:
Addresses #1067 

As expected/discussed, when I have gone to work with the "real" runtimes, I need more than runtime ID to be able to provide a runtime from the extension on demand. My current best idea is that we should store the whole runtime metadata when we do a workspace affiliation. From my initial exploration, this will let us provide R/Python runtimes as we hope to.

This works well with a fresh/new workspace as far as I can tell, but if you have an existing workspace affiliation stored from when we have been using a single string only (`runtimeId`) then Positron gets _very unhappy_. I need to work more on the case of existing affiliations, like with try/catch or similar.

title: Test the `positron-code-cells` extension
description:
I did this in part to figure out how we can test bundled extensions. Here's what I learned (happy to store this elsewhere if it's helpful):

Since the PR https://github.com/microsoft/vscode/pull/195570, the way to test a bundled extension is:

1. Add it to the `extensions` array in the root `.vscode-test.js` file.
2. Ensure that your project has the `@types/mocha` package as a dev dependency (`yarn add -D @types/mocha`). You don't need to include `mocha` itself as a (dev) dependency in your project, since we run tests from the root `positron` project.
3. Create some test files.
    1. The convention appears to be to store tests under `src/test` and to name test files with the suffix `.test.ts`. Although, I think any file that gets compiled to `out/**/*.test.js` will work.
    2. Define tests in your test files with the `suite` and `test` functions provided by Mocha.
4. Once you have some tests defined, you should be able to run them with `yarn test-extension -l {extension-name}`. You can also run `yarn test-extension` to test all bundled extensions – **we _might_ want to include this in our CI**.

---

The `vscode-python` extension quite heavily uses mocks via the `sinon`, `typemoq`, and `ts-mockito` npm packages. But, I noticed that vscode core tests as well as bundled extensions don't seem to do that. They rarely mock, and instead test directly against the VSCode API, which seems to have worked fine for me as well. There do use `sinon` in a few of the core vscode tests.

title: Second wave of R test explorer improvement (eg better "run all tests")
description:
The main user-perceivable change here is that "run all of the tests" is no longer slow. This was brought up in [#1763](https://github.com/posit-dev/positron/pull/1763#discussion_r1389611432) when @DavisVaughan saw the dplyr tests take > 2 mins to run, whereas plain old `devtools::test()` took 35s. We now recognize this case and also route it through `devtools::test()`.

But I also basically made a second pass through all of the testing code and made other improvements/fixes:

* It's now explicit that the testing feature only anticipates the case where the first workspace folder is the root directory of an R source package. Fixing the package (directory) to be tested at feature load time eliminates a lot of janky filepath handling.
  - Fixes #1839
  - Addresses a bullet in #1808
  - If/when we relax this, we only need do so in 1 place. E.g. if we decide it's OK for the R package to be located in a subfolder of the first workspace folder or if we're willing to look through multiple workspace folders for an R package.
* Output from the test run that is not from our custom reporter is now ignored, instead of causing an error and a halt. This sort of noise is very common in R packages (I banged my shins on this in manual testing).
* Rationalized test item IDs, which is a bullet from #1808
* If we receive results for an unrecognized test item, we now log that as an error in the output channel, but soldier on with the test run. Motivated by dplyr's "special" test that has a `paste0()` call in its `desc` instead of a string.

title: Handle bidirectional scrolling and loading of discontinuous chunks of data
description:
This PR allows for the loading of discontinuous chunks of data, namely when scrolling really fast through a somewhat large data frame. We do this by adding support for bidirectional scrolling/data requests, allowing for the data pages to come in out of order (for example if you scroll down fast, and then up again, you may fetch data for page 0, page 10, and then page 6), padding the sparsely fetched data with placeholder rows to ensure proper dimensions and scroll positions, using the current scroll position to determine what page (or pages) of data need to be fetched, and debouncing when the requests are made on scroll change. 

I've also added a request queue on the frontend and backend here, but frankly the queue isn't really doing any work here, rather than ignoring or canceling outdated requests, we're simply not making those requests. But I don't necessarily think there's a harm to leaving it in, it is at the very least useful for making sure we don't double-process requests. 

I also was able to do a pretty substantial refactoring and gutting of the code, including getting rid of the DataModel class entirely (because we actually only ever work with fragments) and removing some pieces of state that made things harder to keep track of and triggered unnecessary re-renders.

One thing that is not addressed here is good handling of variable height rows, which we need to support, but for the meantime I'm making a lot of strong assumptions about constant size rows, which I can address in a follow on PR, however I think it's too much to add to this PR. 

This is by no means foolproof -- I think there are definitely improvements we can make on how we calculate the current scroll page (and handling when the top and bottom of the viewport are on different pages, which is mostly handled here but maybe could be improved). It works reasonably well for Zed, haven't really tested in R and Python because of the limitations on variable height rows mentioned above, but these are pretty much entirely frontend changes.

Addresses #1706

title: Add the `positron-code-cells` extension to support Jupyter/knitr-spin cells in Python/R scripts
description:
This PR adds the `positron-code-cells` extension which provides our own implementation of Jupyter-like code cells in Python scripts, similar to what's provided by the `vscode-jupyter` extension.

Here's a quick demo:

https://github.com/posit-dev/positron/assets/559360/71e0666c-d1f4-4b53-bbe7-931a1af9ed01

Our extension supports the `# %%` format in Python scripts, as well as the knitr spin `#+` format in R scripts.

It offers the same code lenses, commands, key bindings, and cell decorations as the Quarto extension – which I believe is much more user-friendly than `vscode-jupyter`. Rather than executing to `vscode-jupyter`'s "Interactive Window", it executes in the Positron Console.

Addresses #1160, #1430, and #1431.

title: Address problems with `selectRuntime` shutdown/start timing
description:
Joint work with @DavisVaughan 

Addresses #1573 

The main problem causing the bad behavior we observe in that issue ⤴️ is that we commonly end up with this sequence:

- Old runtime starts shutting down
- It get to `Exited` before all the stuff in `onDidEndSession` is finished happening
- New runtime starts because old runtime gets to `Exited`
- Messages about new runtime say "restarting" / "restarted" because the console knows about the previous exit but doesn't know that exit was for a different runtime
- The *new* runtime is running when some things in `onDidEndSession` happen, so the button never gets cleaned up, the message about shutting down uses the wrong runtime, etc

This PR as of right now makes two changes:

- Pass the runtime name as part of the `exit` object so we emit the right message (no longer looking up the current runtime)
- Add another listener plus `Promise.race()` for `onDidEndSession`, to wait until those things are done before starting the new runtime

As of right now, the restart button still gets added (because the old runtime does in fact shutdown) but it is now cleaned up, and the messages are better but not ideal. I can work on these further issues but I wanted to raise a question here first:

#### How confident are we that the right runtime state for _during_ `onDidEndSession` is `Exited`? i.e. are we sure about it firing _after_ the exit is done?

title: Initialise number of log lines seen to support refresh
description:
Follow-up to https://github.com/posit-dev/positron/pull/708 which adds a mechanism to flush the tail of the log on restart. I noticed some missing log lines in case of refresh. This PR fixes this by initialising the number of lines seen from the existing file.

There is a race condition here since the kernel is concurrently writing to the log file. If this happens there will be duplicate lines in the tail of the log when the runtime restarts, but no missing lines.

In addition:

- Rewrite implementation to use a synchronous file access API instead of asynchronous.
- Keep track of error lines seen.

title: Revert "Trigger quick suggest on backspace too"
description:
Reverts https://github.com/posit-dev/positron/pull/1502
Addresses https://github.com/posit-dev/positron/issues/1563

As seen by https://github.com/posit-dev/positron/issues/1563, it has turned out to be much more annoying to have backspace trigger quick suggestions when you don't want them to than it is for a typo to cause your current quick suggestions session to disappear. Not being able to print out the source of an R function due to this is highly annoying.

So this rolls back https://github.com/posit-dev/positron/pull/1502.

In the original report, the complaint was that typing `testthat::expect_c` gave completions, but then adding `ab` caused the completion session to "die", so when you backspaced back to `testthat::expect_c` you no longer got completions. With the new addition of `Tab` as a way to re-trigger quick suggestions, I think this is much less annoying than it was before, so I don't think rolling this back hurts much.

In the future, one alternative to look into is why the completions session is dying in the first place, if we kept it alive even though there are 0 suggestions, then backspace would pull the existing session back up without needing to retrigger a new one. - although honestly the new behavior with this PR + Tab doesn't feel bad to me anymore

title: Implement quick suggest on `Tab`
description:
Addresses https://github.com/posit-dev/positron/issues/1166

New `tabSuggest` editor option that allows `"on"` or `"off"` (using an enum like `tabCompletion` now does, it was a boolean but they got a 3rd option of `onlySnippets` and I want to avoid any backwards compat weirdness if we also get more options in the future).

Defaults to `"on"` because I think we pretty much all want this. I think it is starting to feel _really_ good.

- Respects `Tab Completions`, a new ish VS Code feature that actually inserts the top quick suggest suggestion and then lets you tab your way through the remaining suggestions. We defer to `Tab Completions` if it is turned on by the user, it is off by default. These two features are at odds with each other.
- Respects `Tab Focus Mode`, an accessibility feature that allows the workbench to get `Tab` presses for navigation purposes. It is off by default.
- Respects tab in snippets, allowing you to bounce between snippet placeholders
- Respects selections, i.e. if you highlight part of a word and hit tab, you want an actual tab
- Respects the case of "no leading text", i.e. when there is no non-whitespace text on the line or if the line is `|foo()` with the cursor at the `|`, in which case we insert an actual tab

This ends up respecting most of the same cases that RStudio does, at least from some testing that I've been doing.

---

`tabSuggestContextKey.ts` is modeled after `wordContextKey.ts`, which is used to determine whether `tabCompletion` should be considered active or not. I also borrowed most of the `precondition`s from `insertBestCompletion` (i.e. tab completion) as well, since it has many of the same quirks about exactly when it should be active.
https://github.com/posit-dev/positron/blob/feature/tab-quick-suggest/src/vs/editor/contrib/suggest/browser/wordContextKey.ts
https://github.com/posit-dev/positron/blob/c70751092c5110c9d9665ea4d720dae433143e94/src/vs/editor/contrib/suggest/browser/suggestController.ts#L1049-L1067

---

Does _not_ currently handle the fact that `Tab` in the Console will move you _out_ of the Console when there is no text in the console. I think this should just work like RStudio and insert an actual tab character. It seems like a separate issue though.
https://github.com/posit-dev/positron/issues/1166#issuecomment-1731883180

---

Something I learned while tinkering is that VS Code actually does not respect Tab Focus Mode when Tab Completions is also set. It will prioritize Tab Completions instead. Based on the description of Tab Focus Mode, I think this is a bug. I think Tab Focus Mode should always have highest priority because it is an accessibility feature that seems to be quite important.

title: Introduce a (log) output channel for the R extension
description:
Addresses #1544 

This PR creates a new "logging-flavored" output channel for the R extension. It's deliberately minimal. I even got rid of the `logging.ts` file! I figure we can build back up if/as needed.

Links re: the development of `vscode.LogOutputChannel`, which is new-ish:
* https://code.visualstudio.com/updates/v1_72#_log-output-channel
* https://code.visualstudio.com/updates/v1_73#_log-output-channel

Behaviours worth noting for `vscode.LogOutputChannel`:
* Syntax highlighting.
  I think this is some sort of default "log" highlighting, which isn't beautiful, but better than nothing.
  - I frequently *don't* see the colors upon first load, but only after a reload. I suspect/hope this is a VS Code problem that will self-resolve (maybe this? https://github.com/microsoft/vscode/issues/192115). Or maybe a dev vs. release issue?
* Support for a log level.
  User can control the log level via "Developer: Set Log Level ..." in the command palette:
  - https://code.visualstudio.com/updates/v1_73#_setting-log-level-per-output-channel
  - For the complete product, e.g. Positron, or for the R extension specifically.
  - "On the fly" changes persist after a reload.
  - To get persistence across true restarts, change the default log level by clicking the double check marks in the UI.
  - https://code.visualstudio.com/updates/v1_76#_configure-default-log-level
  - Default log levels are not stored in `settings.json`, but rather in `argv.json`, the runtime arguments JSON file.

This PR also removes previous special arrangements for logging related to setup for the client side of the ARK LSP. However, I don't think we lose any actual functionality.

* The LSP *server* continues to use the "Positron R Language Server (x.y.z)" channel, as before, even though that was not our intention. I comment more on this inline.
* The `positron.r.trace.server` setting continues to control the verbosity of the LSP server's output.
* The messages re: LSP setup from the client side now show up in our new output channel.

Links for any future soul who revisits log output channels:

* Main issue about the development of this feature in VS Code: https://github.com/microsoft/vscode/issues/159892
* When the typescript extension updated itself: https://github.com/microsoft/vscode/issues/176479

title: Which of this language configuration sparks joy?
description:
This is related to this bit of discussion in #1407:

> **Reduce** how much formatting we try to do through language config, like `increaseIndentPattern` rules (we currently have a lot of language config compared to other projects, and we think we're trying to do too much with this blunt tool)

Specifically it removes a fair amount of `onEnterRules` because they don't play nicely with some editor defaults. This will move our R language configuration more into the mainstream of how folks use these features. 

It addresses #1316 and we no longer get INFINITE INDENTATION in dplyr pipelines, ggplot2 pipelines, etc. We will need to add back in how to get indentation right for some of these more special situations via a method that gives us more information about the document as a whole. I'm going to keep this draft until I have another solution to show.

title: Handle `""` separately from `undefined` in `StatementRangeProvider`
description:
Merges into https://github.com/posit-dev/positron/pull/1627

The diff looks more annoying than it is. The 3rd commit removes 1 layer of nesting that is no longer needed since we know `code` is _definitely_ a string at that point, so you could just look at the 2nd commit and mostly ignore that.

---

When working on https://github.com/posit-dev/amalthea/pull/126 I learned that if the statement range provider returns `""` back then it basically gets ignored on the Positron side and we try and execute the current line instead. This is problematic for stepping through roxygen2 lines. Because it steps through the roxygen2 lines one at a time you are bound to hit empty `#'` lines where the leading `#'` gets stripped, leaving you with `""` which we send back as `code`, but we _do_ want this to be respected, as otherwise Positron tries to run the current line containing the full `#'`. This makes executing something like:

```r
#' function() {
#'    x <- 1
#'    
#'    x
#' }  
```

particularly annoying because it will send a `#'` when you are in the middle of executing the function one line at a time.

I've changed the execute statement code so that it defaults the `code` to `undefined` rather than `""` and now respects _anything_ the range provider returns, even `""`.

title: `rawLog` option for `OutputChannel` to colourise the Ark log
description:
I would like to have colourised output in our Ark log because it is currently hard to read. VS Code doesn't support ansi escapes in output channels (see wontfix issue https://github.com/microsoft/vscode/issues/571) but it does colourise output channels that are created with `log: true`.

We can't do the latter option however because that automatically adds timestamps (which we already add elsewhere) and misleading `[info]` tags. I found a way to prevent VS Code from adding these with a new option. Using this, the Ark output becomes much more readable:

https://github.com/posit-dev/positron/assets/4465050/7bf4dfde-929b-41bc-a2c0-3c378bc5ca89


However this requires changing a bunch of VS Code signatures to thread the option in. Is this too much @jmcphers?

title: Runtime notebook controller
description:
This PR adds a new extension `positron-notebook-controllers` which registers a `NotebookController` for each unique language that has a Positron runtime registered. Each notebook controller maintains a unique runtime instance per notebook document.
  
  A few changes were made to Positron core to facilitate this:
  
  1. Added a `clone` method to `positron.LanguageRuntime`, which creates a new instance of a runtime with the `metadata` passed as an argument.
  2. Added the `positron.runtime.getPreferredRuntime(languageId)` function, which gets the "preferred" runtime for a language i.e. the currently running runtime, or if no runtimes are running, the first registered one. This matches the existing logic for the interpreter picker (defined in `createInterpreterGroups` in `interpreterGroups.tsx`), which we _may_ want to refactor to use the same code path.
  3. Added the positron.runtime.onDidRegisterRuntime` event, which fires when a new runtime is registered with Positron. We need to know this in the notebook controller extension in order to detect a new language and register a corresponding notebook controller.

     I'm currently also using this event to build up a set of known runtimes in the notebook controllers, since `getPreferredRuntime` returns only the runtime's metadata, but we need the runtime instance. But this is a hack. Maybe we could expose a `positron.runtime.getRuntime(runtimeId)` function instead?

There are still a few things to do before this is really useable, but I wanted to create a draft PR to get feedback and agree on the minimum version we're happy to merge.

Major items:

1. Language server clients are crashing in this PR. I haven't yet figured out why. I suspect that we may have to implement notebook document support in our language servers, or use the [vscode-jupyter-lsp-middleware](https://github.com/microsoft/vscode-jupyter-lsp-middleware) package.
2. Plots don't always work since our kernels send them over the plots comm instead of a usual Jupyter display data message. We'll need to update the kernels to detect when they're in "notebook mode" (e.g. based on whether the frontend comm has connected) and modify their plotting behaviour in that case.
3. Should cells be executed in a queue? Currently, if you queue a few long-running cells, the follow-up cells don't show as "pending" as they should. Also, if you interrupt a cell at the beginning of the "queue", the rest still execute but shouldn't.
4. Should the notebook runtime survive a browser refresh? It currently does not.
    - Similarly, should the execution order survive a browser refresh?
5. Notebook runtimes should still be connected to the Environment pane.

Minor items:

1. Each controller is named after the language with no version or path info. We should expose an `onDidChangePreferredRuntime` event, and update each notebook controller's detail to match the preferred runtime's name/version at all times.
2. When a notebook controller is selected, should we update all cells to match that controller's language?

title: Don't switch back to Idle too early after interrupt
description:
Part of #1422.

The R runtime is currently switching back to Idle too early after an interrupt, which prevents Positron from detecting unresponsive interrupts. The cause is that the `interrupt()` method of the runtime adapter switches back to Idle as soon as the `interrupt()` method of the Jupyter kernel resolves. However, this currently resolves right after sending the 0MQ message. The fix is as follow:

- The runtime adapter is currently in charge of dealing with concurrent status messages from Shell and Control. I think this logic should be the Jupyter kernel however so I moved it there. Otherwise status messages from Shell and Control interfere with each other.

- IIUC a properly functioning kernel should send an Idle event from Shell when the interrupt has been processed. So we no longer switch back to Idle from the `interrupt()` method in the adapter and we no longer purge the stacks of status messages upon interrupt. Instead, we let the regular status handler switch us back to Idle.

- We no longer clear the status stacks in `interrupt()` but we do clear them in `start()`, in case of (possibly forced) restarts.

I've also added a FIXME regarding the promise resolution of the interrupt. We could either resolve after receiving an `interrupt_reply` (see #1576) or after the interrupt has been processed, which is when the runtime switches back to Idle. I think the latter makes more sense?

title: R: Executing code with Windows line endings
description:
This is no longer just an exploration but is a proposed solution for #1520. Relative to the initial exploratory PR, this:

* Moves all "replace CRLF with LF" into the R runtime, because AFAICT we are only suffering from Windows line endings with R code right now.
* Applies the fix in two places:
  - `isCodeFragmentComplete()`: this parses code, in the form of a string, to determine if we have submitted a complete expression.
  - `execute()`: this executes code, also provided as a string. And executing means parsing.

I went through a phase of thinking the only solution was to expose the user's code to R's parser via a connection. Why? Because, unlike text input, a connection is guaranteed to cope with both CRLF and LF line endings. But this would require a fairly significant change in how we prepare code for the R kernel.

I was worried that simply replacing CRLF with LF would mangle literal `\r\n` in R code. But in the process of trying to prove that the simple approach could not work, I concluded that it does work.

*I'm still working on this.*

title: Improve plots thumbnail experience in Console
description:
This change improves the plots thumbnail experience in the Console. In particular:

- Thumbnails are now a little larger.
- Thumbnails are no longer width-constrained (except by the width of the console), so filmstrip-shaped plot thumbnails are possible (see #1399 for an example)
- Hovering over a thumbnail will reveal it to be a click target (with a border, pointer cursor, and inspect icon). Clicking it will reveal the plot in the Plots pane.

I would still like to do more here; in particular I think that it would be nice to have a better experience if the plot is already selected in the pane since in this case it looks like nothing is happening. Maybe we could show a kind of 100% zoom version of the plot with options to copy to clipboard or save to disk. 

Addresses https://github.com/posit-dev/positron/issues/1399.

title: Ensure inserted operators have a space on right and left
description: Addresses #1318 This PR is intended to ensure `->` and `|>` have a space on the left and the right (except in the weird edge case when the cursor/selection is at the start of the line). Good news: * Works for multiple cursors, in the editor and the console. * Leaves the cursor on the right, even if selection was made in the other direction. Bad news: * The console input's code editor widget is no longer reachable through `vscode.window.activeTextEditor` (#1212), so a temporary move is to create Console-specific arrangements, until #1507 gives us better options. If I don't do this, invoking the commands/keybindings in the console causes the operator to be inserted in the editor (!!), which is bizarre. * In the console, we fall back to inserting a fixed string, regardless of surrounding whitespace. https://github.com/posit-dev/positron/assets/599454/291e016b-34f6-413f-b9f0-af895cf87b7b BTW I'm a believer in "trim trailing whitespace on save", so I'm basically assuming that people who care about such things will have `files.trimTrailingWhitespace": true`.

title: Implement `quickSuggestionsMinimumLength`
description:
This PR is an idea I had to implement a minimum word length required before quick suggestions are triggered. It builds on the idea of the `quickSuggestionsDelay` that already exists in VS Code.

I've defaulted this to requiring 3 characters within the current _word_ before quick suggestions are triggered. This is the same as RStudio from what I can tell, and I think it makes for a less hectic autocompletion experience. I mention that it is 3 characters within the current _word_. This is pretty neat. VS Code has already built in the ability to determine that when you type `function(x, fo|` and your cursor is at the end of `fo`, then really the "word" you are on is `fo` rather than everything that comes before that.

It is configurable through a new editor option and has a range of `[1, 10]`.

I do have a few things I need advice on, and I'll mention those with additional inline comments.


https://github.com/posit-dev/positron/assets/19150088/bbbe3def-98ba-4a26-a96b-d9487db2b4df

Note that this does _not_ get in the way of trigger characters AFAICT, like `.` in Python:

https://github.com/posit-dev/positron/assets/19150088/660280f7-1796-4d54-817e-deec87618345

You can also still _force_ completions to pop up through a manual `Ctrl + Space` (hopefully eventually `Tab`) 

https://github.com/posit-dev/positron/assets/19150088/29c953cd-ea63-4281-b960-90a46ccdc13e

title: Don't focus editor on debugger breaks by default
description:
By default VS Code moves the focus to the editor when a debugger break is hit (either a breakpoint starting a new session or a step command pausing immediately to the next execution step). This is problematic in Positron for two reasons:

- In R, users might interact with the debugger (step over, step in, etc) via the console (sending `n`, `s`, etc) instead of a keybinding or the debug toolbar. In that case moving the focus away really gets in the way of the user workflow.

- When debugging REPL programs, interacting with the runtime by evaluating expressions in the console is very common. This can be done equivalently from the editor or from the console and whichever location the user has chosen to interact with the runtime shouldn't have focus stolen away on break.

To fix this, the PR changes the default of the editor focus setting to `false`. Addresses #1440.

title: Ensure we always "step" down the page when advancing the statement range cursor position
description:
Addresses https://github.com/posit-dev/positron/issues/1463

This PR fixes 2 issues with the statement range provider, and I think it is best to look at the commits individually:

---

f4e8891 addresses https://github.com/posit-dev/positron/issues/1463 by tweaking our behavior when we find our `nextStatement`. Rather than simply accepting it and always moving to its starting row, we are now careful to never move "up" the page, as that results in a jumpy experience for the user.

If the starting row of the "next" statement is _after_ the current statement, then this is the typical "stepping through the code" case that occurs at the top level.

Otherwise, we are probably exiting a nested scope of some kind (like executing the last line of a function or testthat block, as shown in the video of https://github.com/posit-dev/positron/issues/1463), so instead we attempt to move to the _ending_ row of the "next" statement if it is after the current statement.

Otherwise if both of those fail then we are probably (?) in some really broken scenario (i can't think of any examples) so I think the best thing to do is to throw out the `nextStatement` altogether and just move to the next line.

I don't think the Python range provider can currently look "up", so this doesn't really affect it right now.

https://github.com/posit-dev/positron/assets/19150088/2eccbf07-fd20-495e-a482-a16bcd597e1c

---

32aa254 addresses an issue where executing a statement at the end of the document would add a new line, but would not move to it, so you end up executing the statement two times in a row. I've tweaked `amendNewlineToEnd()` so that it _just_ does the edit operation (rather than also doing the "undo" of the move) - now anyone who calls this function is in charge of positioning the cursor appropriately after the fact. ab2693f does a little extra clean up on top of this.

Before:

https://github.com/posit-dev/positron/assets/19150088/50eef27e-7ea0-4b71-9f4f-89bf0905ffa8

After:

https://github.com/posit-dev/positron/assets/19150088/f422a672-9f7b-44b1-b1ae-3ae18781d1f4
